News.title: Labour set to deploy 2,000 new anti-fraud specialists to clampdown on benefits cheats
News.content:
Next

CHANCELLOR John Healey will deploy 2,000 new anti-fraud specialists as part of a major clampdown on benefits cheats.

Officers will be put in Jobcentres to spot suspicious Universal Credit claims early — which is hoped to save £1.4billion.



These employees will work closely with existing staff that handle benefit claims.

Mr Healey’s move, to be announced at the Budget, comes as he faces growing pressure to cut the welfare bill, which is forecast to hit £400billion at the start of the next decade.



Trials have already started, with one claimant’s application rejected for using a digitally altered document and giving conflicting accounts of their ability to work.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “We need to make the most of every pound of taxpayers’ money and cut fraud to ensure the welfare system is fair and sustainable. We’re rooting out those who abuse the system, while protecting those who need it most.”

Currently, 78 staff are working on the project, rising to 250 by the end of the year and 2,000 by 2030.

Mr Healey will also be targeting “abroad fraud” where people claim taxpayer cash after leaving the UK. One individual held on to £39,000 despite living in Zimbabwe.

But the welfare blitz comes after Sir Keir Starmer climbed down from his own attempted reforms due to a backbench rebellion.

A key priority for the overhaul will be the nearly one million Neets aged 16-24 who are not currently in education, employment, or training.



Meanwhile, the Budget will also see Mr Healey unveil an AI safety package to guard against cyber threats.

This will include £165million going to an AI Biosecurity Lab, and £10million to study AI’s impact on jobs.

News.title: Brit mum, 36, who drowned while desperately trying to save her two children in Bahamas snorkelling horror is pictured
News.content:
HOLS TRAGEDY Brit mum, 36, who drowned while desperately trying to save her two children in Bahamas snorkelling horror is pictured







Next

A BRIT mum who drowned while trying to save her two children has been pictured for the first time.

Leanne Gregory, 36, was snorkelling with her family in the Bahamas when a strong current suddenly swept the two youngsters away.



Filled with fear she dived after her two sons in a desperate bid to save them.

But tragically Leanne was pulled unconscious from the water in the horror incident on Tuesday.



Husband Nathan Gregory, 36, tried to resuscitate her as emergency services were called.

Police rushed to the ferry dock in Bimini shortly after 10am – but the mum-of-two had already been taken away for treatment.

Doctors later pronounced her dead.

Her two boys were safely rescued from the water by emergency services.

A spokesman for the Royal Bahamas Police Force said foul play was “not suspected”.

Witness Katie Resciniti wrote on Facebook: “I was there for all of it. She’s a hero.



She added: “Also pray for her husband. He went out to save the other boy but a bystander was able to get him.

“It was truly terrible and nobody’s fault. Just two boys who were eager to get in the water and then things went crazy fast.

“Two of the best parents I’ve ever seen in my entire life.”



The captain of the snorkelling expedition boat Linty Stuart told local news outlet ZNS that he “saw two boys and a mum” in the water but that powerful tides stopped them from being able to reach the mother.

The outlet reported that “one of her children got in distress” when Leanne jumped in to save him.

Speaking to The Telegraph, the boys’ grandma Mrs Jones said: “It is devastating. Leanne drowned trying to save her two boys who got into trouble in choppy waters.

“They can both swim, they’re good swimmers, but the current was too strong”, she added.

Giving a heartbreaking detail, she said: “Nathan tried to save her, by giving her the kiss of life. Sadly, it was too late.”



The husband’s dad and brother are flying out to support the family, according to Nathan’s nephew Gail Parker.

The family lived in Stapleford, Nottinghamshire and had been on holiday in the Bahamas over half term.

Nathan and Leanne were childhood sweethearts who had been together for more than 20 years, having first met in school.

A spokesman for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”



At least four people have drowned off the coast of hols hotspot Bimini since 2024.

News.title: Andy Burnham says booze shouldn’t be a priority in an emergency kit in case of attack by Russia
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has warned Brits not to prioritise booze in their emergency rations in case of a Russian attack.

But they can still have a “glass or two” to help them deal with the stress.



Minister Angela Rayner had joked a bottle of sauvignon blanc and mascara would be in her stash.

Quizzed on BBC Radio 5 Live, the PM said wine should not be your “best first port of call” in a crisis.



He added: “It probably helps when you’ve done the hard work, but I’ll stick to the basics, I think.”

On his own top picks for emergency supplies, he said: “I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.



“I think those are the kinds of things I would recommend people to have. As well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by without those for too long.”

Houses are being told to stock up on long-lasting food, water, cash, and medicines in case of an attack or natural disaster.



The warning was reiterated more strongly this week, as government and business websites were taken down to address cyber-security flaws.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting urged people to be ready and has been launching a “national resilience conversation”.

Military bigwigs will address the nation in the coming days to explain why we need to spend more on defence, Mr Streeting added.



He spoke again about the “Be Ready” campaign at a new factory in Shropshire where Britain will be producing parts for tanks for the first time in 20 years.

News.title: Police officer raped by serial predator David Carrick calls for Met chief to quit after ordeal left her ‘suicidal’
News.content:
Next

A POLICE officer raped by a fellow cop has called for the Met’s chief to resign.

Linda Williams, 60, was attacked by ex-armed officer David Carrick.



The 51-year-old fiend is serving 37 life sentences after admitting 71 sexual offences, including 48 rapes.

DC Williams, who has waived her right to anonymity, says she was driven to contemplate suicide because of the way she was treated by the London force throughout her legal claim.



Her case against the Met — now led by Sir Mark Rowley — has been settled for six figures without them admitting liability.

But she said: “The process has taken me right back to how I felt when I was raped by Carrick: controlled, abused and powerless.

“If I was raped tomorrow, I wouldn’t report it.

“At no point did I feel the police sincerely acknowledged I had been through a horrific sexual attack and that the trauma had deeply scarred me, or their role in it all.”

She added: “The Met needs to set up a unit overseen by victims, like me, who understand what it’s like to be raped. For this to happen, Rowley needs to go.”

The Met said it “tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams” and that Sir Mark had met her.



It added: “David Carrick should never have been a police officer.

“We are truly sorry for the harm and suffering he caused his victims.”

News.title: Tackling benefit cheats is a start, Chancellor – now take a sledgehammer to the bloated welfare system
News.content:
Benefits blitz







Next

HATS off to the Chancellor for launching a ferocious new crackdown on benefit cheats plundering the system.

Nearly £10billion is lost every year to fraud and error and John Healey has a moral duty to stop taxpayers’ money being abused.



But he must not kid himself that his Budget blitz will free up enough cash to put debt-plagued Britain on the road to economic recovery.

By his own estimates, 2,000 anti-fraud officers are expected to save £1.4billion — less than 0.5 per cent of the £334billon welfare bill.



This won’t even scratch the surface after last week’s jump in ­inflation added £5.5billion to the tab.

Welfare costs more than any other public service, with the DWP’s massive budget exceeding what we spend on the NHS. But the PM has delayed a decision on cuts until after the Budget.

If Labour is serious, it could get a grip on the ballooning cost of disability and sickness payments to those with low-level mental health conditions, and restrict payments for non-UK citizens.

Tackling fraud is a good start, Chancellor. But until you take a sledgehammer to the bloated system, taxpayers will continue to feel cheated.

Stop dithering

ANDY Burnham is trying desperately to paper over the cracks in his Government on immigration.

The PM says he strongly supports Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s reforms to ensure the right to settle in Britain must be earned.



But he stops short of backing all the changes she has proposed, including making foreign workers wait ten to 15 years instead of five to claim indefinite leave to remain in the UK. Why?

Because he is scared of upsetting 100 left-wing MPs opposed to the change.

The crackdown is needed now to prevent millions who arrived after Brexit from winning permanent status from next year.

Without this move, more than 1.6million migrants will become eligible for settlement, allowing them to claim benefits and access public services.

Burnham should stop dithering, show some leadership and get four-square behind his Home Secretary’s bold plan.



That could work

NEARLY a million young people are stuck on the jobs scrapheap, some facing the grim prospect of a lifetime on benefits.

Many are just looking for their first foothold in the world of work but are prevented from doing so by red tape.

Three million hardworking sole traders want to offer work experience but are choked by £300 insurance bills.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Along with our Jobs Army campaign, Alan Milburn’s plan to let the state back these placements would help small firms and give under-25s a vital start.

Most youngsters don’t want handouts – they just need a foot in the door.

News.title: Democrats are set for good midterms despite their hard Left candidates – but they will need to learn lessons before 2028
News.content:
Next

“WELL, just look at my hat.”

Sitting on the deck of Jason Joyce’s lobster boat, my ­question over his voting ­intentions has not gone down very well.



There’s been a Joyce fishing these waters for eight generations — all the way back to the War of Independence.

Amid trade wars, crippling fuel costs and industry-destroying regulations set by pen-pushers thousands of miles away, whether there will be another is a very live issue in these parts.



Pointing to the outline of the state of Maine on his baseball cap next to the word TAIN, Joyce sighs: “We want to ­maintain. Get it? Maine. Tain.

“Maintain our way of life and maintain some normalcy.”

We’re discussing the Midterm elections next month and the direction of travel of the ­Democrats, who are pushing hard this year to reach rural workers in America’s 9th ­poorest state.

Given how the party nationally has lurched to the Left, picking candidates more concerned with Gaza and men playing in women’s sport, I asked how all that woke stuff lands far away from the urban areas of the country’s­ progressive North East?

“If a man tried to do that with my daughter, I’d wring his neck,” Jason says in a tone that leaves me in no doubt. “We don’t want to go crazy up this way.”

The Senate race here in Maine has generated national headlines after the Democrats’ first candidate — a radical socialist oysterman — withdrew after it emerged he had a Nazi tattoo on his chest and had faced sexual assault claims.

Now they have turned to Troy Jackson who, before a 20-year stint as a politician, claims to have been a logger — albeit one who spent more time on the picket line than cutting down trees.



Backed by the new powerbrokers of the American Left, the Democratic Socialists of America, he rejects the “S” label as he plays up his working-class, rural credentials.

But his radical — for the US, at least — platform of free healthcare for all, abolishing ICE border agents and taxing billionaires, has earned him glowing endorsements from hard-left kingmaker Bernie Sanders and progressive presidential wannabe Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

But Jason is far from alone in his deeply held suspicion of this new offering.



A four-hour drive away into the woods outside tiny East Machias, I ask Eric — a logger who works seven days a week in the winter for an ever-decreasing return — the same question. “How long have you got,” came the blunt reply after a long pause.

Left behind by the richer and snazzier parts of New England, blue-collar Maine exports 41 per cent of its goods to Canada, including huge chunks of its near half-a-billion annual lobster haul and daily shipments of timber.

This is the front line of Donald Trump’s trade wars, and, thanks to surging fuel costs, it feels the heat from his actual wars more than most places.

But in East Machias, a little Trump-backing town towards the Canadian border, the ­President’s share of the vote actually increased in every election since 2016, despite Maine itself staying blue.

There’s little feeling I can detect here that the Democrats are making anywhere near the inroads needed in these working ­communities to force out 30-year Republican Senator Susan Collins.



And Maine is just one ­warning light flashing on the dashboard for the party.

Last week it was the Midwest, where working-class voters, black and white, who were once staunchly Democrat, are also sounding the alarm on the progressive shift.

Detroit community organiser Rev Horace Sheffield can claim to speak more credibly than most on the inner workings of urban voting patterns.

His father was a union ­organiser, his daughter is the Mayor of Detroit.



Aspiring ­politicians in these parts come to pay homage at his church, and not just to the Lord. When Horace says he is worried “the woke stuff” is hitting the Democrats, then party elders and strategists should pay attention.

“Right now, I’m more concerned about what I got to pay for than someone’s sexual orientation,” he told me. “I do think absolutely that part of what has hurt us is that we’ve been seen as people who make some of the more ancillary issues more mainstream than they need to be.”

Yes, heading into November there is obvious anger at Trump, the cost-of-­living crisis and his role in driving up prices. That much is a given.

But are the Democrats in danger of walking into a spectacular trap?



Across the country, the headlines this year have been dominated by loony Left Democrat candidates apologising for their masculinity, or demanding a ban on eating meat, fireworks, Thanksgiving or, even more bizarrely, US football.

Polling consistently shows banning trans men from women’s sport and spaces is supported by 80 per cent of the country, yet the argument still rages.

Abolishing the Senate, neutering the Supreme Court and jailing Elon Musk for being rich might sound great in sports hall debates among the blue-haired brigade, but in the real world, normal people are left scratching their heads.

There’s a real chance the Democrats have a good night on November 3, gaining control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate too.

Such is the anger at the President — be it over Iran, inflation or a growing sense of unease over corruption allegations — they may well win.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

But I can’t help thinking that will be despite some of the hardline candidates they have chosen, not because of them.

If the lesson the party were to draw from victory is that their 2028 election candidate should be cut from the same left-wing cloth, I suspect they are in for a very rude national awakening in two years’ time.

News.title: Razor-wielding barber threatened to kill train passengers during rampage
News.content:
Next

A BARBER who brandished a cut-throat razor on a train while threatening to “kill all the English” and shouting about Jihad has been jailed.

Hogr Saeed, 35, became abusive to passengers on the Southeastern service for Dover Priory after one man asked him to speak quietly on the phone.

Saeed had been drinking alcohol and started shouting at passengers before pulling out and brandishing a cut-throat razor, Canterbury Crown Court heard.

He was arrested at Dover on April 3 and put into a police van where he later spat and urinated.





Saeed was heading to the coast in an attempt to leave the country illegally following a home office meeting, the court heard.

The Iraqi national was said to be “ranting loudly” when a passenger asked him to be quiet.

Prosecutor Surinder Singh Gohlan said: “At 8.45pm the defendant was on a train and became agitated and started shouting at passengers.

“Ms Griffiths, the onboard train manager, was one of those people, and she said he was witnessed to have pulled out and brandished a cut-throat razor, and he said that he was drinking throughout.



“He made threats to customers and staff which included, ‘F*** you’, ‘F*** the English’, ‘Kill all the English on the train’ and ‘I’m going to kill everyone, I’m going to stab you’.”

Saeed also asked passengers if they knew what Jihad meant.

A pair of scissors were found in his possession which, along with the razor, were due to this work as a barber the court heard.

Mr Gohlan said: “The train arrived at Dover Priory.



“He was arrested and a cut-throat razor and a pair of scissors were seized from his bag.

“He said to police ‘I’ll kill you’. The officer reports that the defendant spat on the cell van wall while being transferred to custody and urinated on the cell van floor.”

During his interview the next day, Saeed said the razor was for his job but denied brandishing it.

He admitted to urinating in the police van but added: “he couldn’t control it”.

The court heard a victim impact statement by Laura Griffiths, she said since the incident she had felt unsafe in her job.



The statement continued: “She actively seeks out places of safety. She experiences flashbacks, trouble sleeping, anxiety and feels generally unsafe and threatened.”

Saeed admitted to pleaded guilty to affray and criminal damage in April before later admitting to threats to kill and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place in June.

His mitigating, lawyer Louis Adams said: “Mr Saeed is a man who has spent a significant amount of time remanded in custody.

“The defence expert psychiatrist says Mr Saeed was not feeling well prior to his arrest and in conclusion said that Mr Saeed’s mental health had an impact on his offence.

“He is very sorry for his actions. He expressed remorse and said to me this morning that he wants help with his mental health.



“Your honour would have seen his explanation. He had attended an appointment with the Home Office on the day of offence before travelling to Kent.

“It appears he was upset as it appeared likely he would be deported and he drank alcohol.”

Mr Adams said that a psychiatrist believes Saeed shows symptoms of Schizoaffective disorder.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Saeed was jailed for two years and is now set to be deported.

News.title: England’s oldest boozer finally confirmed as 14th century inn founded by monks as decades of debate are settled
News.content:
Next

ENGLAND’S oldest boozer has finally been identified, ending decades of debate.

Documents show The George Inn at Norton St Philip, Somerset, has held a licence the longest.



Monks had it built in the late 1300s to provide hospitality for merchants visiting their monastery’s markets and fairs.

Analysis shows wood in some of the pub’s frames date from between 1430 and 1432.



Building archaeologist Dr James Wright said many other inns rely on myth to support their claim to be the oldest.

However, paperwork suggests The George was set up by nearby Hinton Priory “as a savvy money-making exercise”.



Dr Wright added that its stone and timber suggest the building has been in use for more than 600 years.

He said: “There are many, many claims to be the oldest pub in the country, yet so few have evidence to back up those claims.

“But the science pinpoints the archaeological development of The George Inn.

“We’re not guessing at its age — that’s the difference between a local legend and a national treasure.”



Dr Wright said: ”To get to the real evidence of these buildings we’ve to look at the fabric, and we’ve got to look at the story of the people who actually built them, and that all leads us to the village of Norton St Philip in Somerset.

”You are now looking at the oldest purpose built inn in England.

Historic England said: “The dates painted on pub signs can be inaccurate, and when evidence is missing imagination often fills the gaps.”

News.title: Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast
News.content:
More than 10,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales, with more bad weather expected this weekend.

The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.

In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.

On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland.

Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal.

Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart".

"The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel.

News.title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018.

In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her.

Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines.

Thomas Markle, who is 82 and based in the US, denies possessing any such images.

Commenting after the allegations, first reported by The Sun newspaper, external, the duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families".

She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children".

News.title: Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father
News.content:
Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.

Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled.

He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze.

He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren.

Now Meghan has told us why.

Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding.

Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery.

There was no lack of drama.

The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren.

From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close.

And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife.

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"Oh bottoms!"

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

News.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
News.content:
A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and his anguish over those he could not save.

Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by parent Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.

"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".

He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.

"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was also killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.

Giamanco told OPB the day of the attack began with breakfast and packed lunches. He and his wife spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.

The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.

He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.

Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.

"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" he told the broadcaster.

He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.

"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.

News.title: Bayern Munich manager Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training
News.content:
Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.

The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.

The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday.

Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital.

"Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external

"The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session.

"Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care.

"His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice."

Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday.

"Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl.

"Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs.

"His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery."

Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game.

German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week".

He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well.

"He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus.

"Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there.

"The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him.

"Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there."

News.title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
News.content:
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

News.title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
News.content:
Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer.

But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial.

Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year.

Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them.

The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored â both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer.

Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive".

"It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said.

"We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival."

The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday.

They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts.

News.title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
News.content:
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.

Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.

But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.

The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.

These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.

The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.

In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.

In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.

But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.

In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.

Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.

The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.

Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.

Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.

Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.

The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.

News.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
News.content:
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
News.content:
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.

The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.

The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.

"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".

She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.

Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.

The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.

It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.

In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.

"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.

At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.

The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."

Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.

She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."

In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."

NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.

"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."

Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.

In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

News.title: Man dies after car crashes into Lidl supermarket
News.content:
A man in his 30s has died after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl shop in Wolverhampton.

Police were called to the supermarket in Finchfield Hill shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday.

West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and a number of other people were treated for injuries.

West Midlands Fire Service said it dispatched four crews to the incident at 17:51 BST with two crews still at the scene at 20:05 BST.

News.title: Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
News.content:
A police force has still not received the Â£2m it was promised by the government in the wake of a car crash that led to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, the local police and crime commissioner (PCC) says.

Cleveland PCC Matt Storey said Cleveland Police was still waiting for the extra funding promised by the home secretary in August.

Shabana Mahmood pledged the cash in light of challenges faced by the force following the deaths, which followed a pursuit on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

The Home Office said the force would receive the Â£2m it had been promised by the end of November.

During the fatal crash, a Volkswagen Passat in which the five young men were travelling hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.

The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - were also killed.

On the morning of the crash, Cleveland Police said it received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 had been seen ramming properties.

Further arrests were subsequently made in connection with organised crime, including the following weekend after another vehicle ramming.

News.title: Trial set for men accused of synagogue bomb plot
News.content:
Two Iranian men have appeared in court over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb.

Salam Ahmadyan, 36, of Liverpool, and Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, are accused of conducting hostile reconnaissance at Heaton Park Synagogue, which was subject to a fatal attack last year, along with the Jewish Museum in Cheetham Hill.

The pair, who arrived illegally into the UK on boats, are charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts on or before 20 September. They deny the charges.

They appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey and a trial date was set at Manchester Crown Court for 15 June 2027.

It is alleged Ahmadyan and Salehi were in contact with an Iranian national who directed and co-ordinated the planned attack, with the third party most likely operating within Iran.

The men are accused of getting instructions to make a chlorine bomb and acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device.

They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.

The pair deny the charges against them.

The trial is estimated to last five weeks. The next court hearing is due to take place on 16 April next year.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue on 2 October last year, and began a knife attack while wearing a fake suicide belt.

News.title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
News.content:
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.

Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than Â£23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.

Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.

Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.

Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".

The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.

The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028.

Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

News.title: Man who fatally struck deputy after his son was killed by Cincinnati police is convicted of murder
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A man who struck and killed a county deputy with his car the day after his teenage son was fatally shot by a Cincinnati police officer was convicted of murder Friday.

Rodney Hinton Jr. was also found guilty of reckless homicide and felonious assault for the crash last year that killed Deputy Larry Ray Henderson Jr. while he was directing traffic for a college graduation. Henderson, who had spent decades working for the Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office, had retired from the department a few months before the crash but was still working off-duty assignments.

Hinton pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. His lawyer, Clyde Bennett II, said he would appeal the conviction.

Hamilton County Sheriff Charmaine McGuffey said the jury's verdict brought some closure and helped provide justice for Henderson.

The case focused heavily on Hinton's mental state during the crash.

Bennett said in closing arguments that Hinton was trying to kill himself when he drove into the intersection and described him as having a psychotic episode. Hinton was also diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and other mental illnesses.

But prosecutors said although he was distraught and grieving, he made the choice to aim his car at the deputy and that his mental illnesses didn't stop him from understanding what was right and wrong.

Hinton faces 15 years to life in prison with the possibility of parole on the murder conviction. Sentencing is scheduled for Nov. 16.

The deadly crash in May 2025 came a few hours after Hinton and other family members watched police body camera footage showing the officer fatally shoot his 18-year-old son, Ryan Hinton.

He was shot twice during a chase. The officer who fired told investigators that the suspect pointed a gun at him, Cincinnati’s police chief has said.

The officer wasn't charged in his death. Hamilton County Prosecutor Connie Pillich said last year that a review of the shooting found that the officer was “legally justified in his use of force.”

Hinton had a fully loaded gun and pointed it at officers when they confronted him, Pillich said.

Henderson had a long career with the Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office. During his funeral last year, he was described as a selfless colleague, dedicated public servant and someone who regularly volunteered for the most dangerous assignments.

News.title: Offenders who breach Respect Orders could face up to two years in jail
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Breaching new anti-social behaviour orders will be a criminal offence from next week and can be punishable by up to two years’ jail, the Home Office said.

The new Respect Orders will allow police and councils to take stronger enforcement action, filling a gap in existing anti-social behaviour powers, the Home Office added.

Under tougher new powers coming into force, repeat anti-social behaviour offenders could be banned from town centres, face curfew bans or be ordered to stop drinking in public hotspots including high streets and local parks.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: “Unchecked, anti-social behaviour blights our communities. But it is not inevitable and I won’t accept it.

“For too long, we have lacked the powers we need to deal with this problem properly. From today, that changes: authorities will be able to take tough action against these offenders.

“This delivers on a commitment we made to the British people in our manifesto. And, most importantly, those who make life a misery for others will now face the consequences of their actions.”

open image in gallery Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said authorities will now be able to take tough action ( PA Wire )

Housing associations and transport networks can apply for a Respect Order, as well as police and local councils.

The orders will only apply to adults, but under-18s can still receive an existing Youth Injunction which includes both prohibitions and requirements.

Catherine Akehurst, the National Police Chiefs’ Council lead for anti-social behaviour, said: “We welcome the new legislation to introduce Respect Orders which will provide police and partner agencies additional tools to tackle anti-social behaviour which we know can so often undermine a sense of safety in communities, erode pride in neighbourhoods, and diminish overall quality of life.

“This new tool will enable swift enforcement against prolific offenders, while prioritising rehabilitation and support to break cycles of criminal and anti-social behaviour.”

The move comes after it was announced earlier this week that people who play music out loud on buses could face fines of up to £1,000.

The push forms part of a wider crackdown on antisocial behaviour across public transport.

Local authorities are being encouraged to use new powers to levy fines for nuisance behaviour on buses, including littering, vaping and listening to music without headphones.

News.title: Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders unionize after years of fighting for higher pay
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders are unionizing.

The NFL franchise has agreed to recognize the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association as the collective bargaining representative for one of the most famous cheer squads in professional sports, both sides said in a joint statement Friday, which follows years of the cheerleaders fighting for pay increases.

“The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for the talent and dedication they exhibit,” the statement said. "They remain one of the most sought-after opportunities for talented dancers worldwide.”

During the second season of the Netflix series “America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders,” which aired last year, one of the cheerleaders said that the members were getting a 400% boost in pay. In 2019, the Cowboys settled a lawsuit with a former cheerleader that led to the squad doubling the per-game pay, from $200 to $400. So the raise announced in 2025 was four times that.

A contact for the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association could not immediately be found on Friday.

The Cowboys have been the most valuable pro sports team in the world, according to Forbes magazine.

News.title: Lunar surface meteor strikes on minds of Nasa bosses in developing Moon base
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nasa chiefs are “giving a lot of thought” to meteor strikes on the lunar surface in ambitious plans to develop a base on the Moon.

Space agency boss Jared Isaacman has said there were going to be potentially hazardous environmental factors that needed to be taken into account in establishing an outpost.

He made his comments after it was revealed, last month, that a comet or asteroid the size of a building up to six-storeys high had crashed into the moon’s surface back in 2024.

The impact left a crater about 728 feet wide and 141 feet deep.

open image in gallery The proposed lunar outpost would provide a continual human presence on the moon (Nasa) ( PA Media )

Scientists have described the magnitude of the collision as a “once-in-a-lifetime” incident, which occurred around every century.

During the Artemis II space mission, earlier this year, around the far side of the Moon, the astronauts aboard observed several flashes as small space rocks, known as meteoroids, slammed directly into the lunar surface at high speeds without an atmosphere to burn them up.

Nasa plans to land people back on the natural satellite in 2028, with a view to having a Moon base up and running by 2032, providing a continual human presence with routine crew rotations.

The pioneering project aims to develop the technologies needed for future deep space voyages, including to Mars.

Nasa is scheduled to launch the Artemis III mission next year.

Four crew members will test low Earth orbit docking procedures between the Orion spacecraft and commercial lunar landers, developed by Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin and Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Mr Isaacman was asked about the implications of the recently discovered asteroid strike on the far-reaching plans for a Moon base during a briefing at the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida, on Friday.

He said: “Fortunately, that’s a once-in-a-century type of an event, so we’re fortunate in that regard.

“But there are much smaller meteor strikes that will happen on the lunar surface with greater frequency.

“We got some additional data from that from the great crew of Artemis II and some of the observations they relayed back during their mission.

“So, we are giving a lot of thought to that for the Moon base.”

Mr Isaacman pointed out a fleet of lunar rovers would be used to scout and map the Moon’s surface and inform the development of the outpost.

He said: “We’re going to learn and we’re going to gradually scale up capabilities because I guarantee you we’re going to need surface improvement.

“It’s why we’re not locking in the design for habitation modules today.

“We’re doing our science of survival, lots of uncrewed robotic landers, lots of demos, see what we like to build up to it.

“Because yes, there are going to be environmental factors we’re going to need to consider that could be hazardous and be able to address them. And we will do it in a logical, iterative way to get to the right outcome.”

Mr Isaacman also said he was impressed at the progress being made by the Blue Origin team, after its rocket dramatically exploded on the launchpad.

The spaceflight company has a key role to play from the outset in the Moon base plans.

The development relies in large part on the heavy-lift New Glenn rocket, which detonated during an engine-firing test at the end of May.

Mr Isaacman said: “I think they’ve been very open about targeting the end of the year… they are moving with purpose.

“So, whether they hit December or they wind up in January, they’re breaking everyone’s records.”

Pressed over whether he would “put money” on landing astronauts on the Moon in 2028, Mr Isaac said: “We are putting taxpayer money on it, but we are doing so in the most efficient, responsible way we possibly can in that regard.”

He acknowledged that “a monumental effort is ahead” and added: “We are very eyes wide open to what needs to be done, and what needs to be done is to get ready to launch Artemis III. And, in parallel, we need to launch a lot of Moon-based missions.”

He added: “This is an achievable path we are on right now.

“We have the mandate, we have the resources, the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do.”

News.title: Tears, Budget, and Strictly anxiety: Andy Burnham becomes first PM to appear on Celebrity Gogglebox
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prime minister Andy Burnham became the first British leader to appear on Celebrity Gogglebox on Friday and fought back tears as he listened to stories of people affected by cancer.

The Channel 4 special for Stand Up To Cancer also featured other celebrities including Devil Wears Prada star Stanley Tucci, the Sugababes, and comedian Joe Lycett.

Mr Burnham was joined on the sofa by his friend Liverpool City mayor Steve Rotherham.

During the one-hour programme, the PM made jokes about Ed Balls, the forthcoming Budget, showcased his knowledge of the roles within the Royal household and bragged about being an English graduate.

Watching an episode of Only Connect, he recalled former shadow chancellor Ed Balls’ appearance on Strictly Come Dancing in 2016.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham fights back tears on Googlebox ( Celebrity Gogglebox )

“I just think of Ed Balls when I hear that,” Burnham said while listening to PSY’s “Gangnam Style”. “I don’t think I can ever get that image out of my mind. You can’t unsee it can you?”

He added: “When I hear this music [Strictly theme tune], I get a pang of anxiety. And I’ll tell you why, because I did this for the great Rob Burrow. Never, ever again.”

Answering questions about appointments in the Royal household, Burnham expressed confidence, saying: “I should get this”.

With the help of Mr Rotherham he answered questions on the titles (Warden of the Swans and Keeper of the Privy Purse) correctly.

“The King will be pleased with me when I see him for my audience next week,” he said. But he admitted he did not know who the Keeper of the Privy Purse was. “I should know that shouldn’t I?”

open image in gallery Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she was ‘amazed’ Burnham had the time ( PA Wire )

Working out a maths question on the same show, he joked: “I’ll be alright at the Budget.” Both Rotherham and Burnham drank a beer and ate crisps, including pork scratchings.

He showed a more sombre side and appeared to fight back tears hearing the story of 16-year-old Callum who died from a rare form of cancer.

However, politicians were unimpressed with his appearance with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and a Green party councillor hitting out at Mr Burnham for choosing to appear on the show.

Ms Badenoch said she was “amazed” that he had time to do the programme.

"What I'm amazed at is that Andy Burnham has got time to go on Gogglebox," she said.

"When you get a new job in politics it's so difficult. There's so much to do and it's like drinking from a fire hose.

"Even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state I never had time to go on Gogglebox - I just don't know how he's got the time. Gogglebox takes hours to do."

open image in gallery Burnham was joined by his friend and Liverpool City mayor Steve Rotherham ( Channel 4/Gogglebox )

Green Party councillor Florence Schecter called the appearance “ridiculous” in an interview on LBC. “Is that a really good use of his time?”

She said: “A third of British children are living in poverty and he’s going on Gogglebox.”

The sentiments were echoed online with several viewers making comments online including one person who called it a “cringeworthy stunt”. Others said that the programme was part of Mr Burnham’s role as a public figure.

The prime minister defended himself against the criticism telling BBC Radio 5 Live: "It is always a moment in the annual calendar where we support Stand Up To Cancer through Gogglebox. Steve and I are proud to do it. I'm trying to give the country a lift - trying to give the country some hope.

"That's always my approach and it's what I'm trying to do. It may not appeal to everybody when it comes to Gogglebox.

"It's Stand Up To Cancer night and I've always been somebody who puts my shoulder behind the fight against cancer."

News.title: Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy
News.content:
A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

News.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears of fresh strikes on Iran
News.content:
The price of oil has hit a five-month high amid fears Donald Trump will ramp up strikes in the Middle East following the midterm elections.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed as much as 2.8pc to more than $116 a barrel, pushing down stock markets in the US and Europe.

It followed a New York Times report that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections.

Oil has climbed more than 4pc this week, increasing pressure on stock markets at the same time as fears grow about the valuations of AI companies.

European shares fell on Friday, with the FTSE 100 down as much as 0.8pc, the Cac 40 in Paris down 1pc and the Dax in Frankfurt down 1.1pc.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell as much as 1pc, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell at a slower pace than the previous day.

Traders were rattled on Thursday after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of the technology.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq in New York dropped by 2.6pc on Thursday while the S&P 500 fell 1.2pc on its worst day since July.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta was one of the worse hit in the sell-off, as its shares finished trading almost 7pc lower.

Overnight, the sell-off spread into Asian markets. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week.

The Kospi index in South Korea declined as much as 4.1pc on Friday but recovered to be marginally higher as markets closed.

The stock market turmoil led to a jump in safe haven assets like bonds.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, a benchmark for the cost of borrowing for governments around the world, fell by the largest amount since March 2023.

News.title: Europe’s record-breaking summer heat estimated to have killed 50,000 people
News.content:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe as a result of this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves, according to research.

In the UK alone, researchers estimate there were 4,354 excess deaths this summer.

The number of excess deaths across Europe is double the number recorded in 2025 and it is also far higher than the previous record of 29,000 deaths. This was recorded in 2022 when the continent also endured exceptionally high temperatures, with the mercury hitting 40 degrees celsius for the first time in the UK.

According to the Met Office the UK saw its hottest ever summer this year with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Mainland Europe experienced its third hottest summer, with temperatures particularly high in the south and west.

Researchers from Imperial College, London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) looked at 854 urban areas in 30 countries across Europe. Using temperature records and modelling based on the relationship between heat and mortality they estimated the number of heat-related deaths that occurred between June and August.

They said findings from previous years’ excess heat mortality modelling matched official figures released later by national health authorities.

Because the study only looked at urban areas – making up 40 per cent of the population of the countries studied – researchers believe the number of deaths is likely to be an underestimate.

According to the study, published in Nature Health, southern and western Europe were hardest hit. Italy experienced the highest number of excess deaths (13,303), followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) then the UK.

There were an estimated 22,000 deaths among those aged 85 and over but researchers pointed out that an estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are also likely to have died as a result of the heat.

Around a third of the deaths took place in late June, when average temperatures across Europe were more than 5°C above what would be expected during this time of year. Researchers say in early summer people were less likely to have acclimatised to the sweltering weather. This period was marked by both extremely high humidity and unusually high night-time temperatures, making it difficult for people to cool down.

Researchers also estimated that more than two thirds of the total excess deaths were attributable to climate change. Across the continent as a whole Europe was an average 2.9°C higher than would have been expected. However, in some places temperatures were as much as 12°C higher.

Dr Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College, said extreme heat was having a severe impact on public health.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

Dr Pierre Masselot, assistant professor of statistics and epidemiology at LSHTM and one of the study’s authors, said “climate change is everybody’s problem”.

“It is not just hot regions that are suffering any more with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden. And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

“It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation. This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.”

News.title: Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history
News.content:
Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

News.title: Harry Brook hits historic double century – but England still lose to Sri Lanka
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to the fourth match of the autumn tri-series in Pakistan. After two wins for the hosts, the two touring sides face each other for the first time in Rawalpindi, the last match here before the circus leaves for Lahore. England and Sri Lanka played each other only last month in this format, England winning at Chester-le-Street and the Oval by a distance, those victories sandwiching a narrow defeat at Headingley where, if you remember, Harry Brook’s side were cruising until Jos Buttler ripped his left hamstring. He did eventually come back out to bat on one leg as his rattled team-mates flapped and fell to Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga.

On Tuesday against Pakistan, England again were flying with both ball and bat but they let the middle-order rebuild, losing control of the rate. Their two most experienced white-ball bowlers, Adil Rashid, who looked rusty after breaking his hand in August, and Sam Curran, who missed the end of August and all of September following groin surgery, went for 6.87 and eight runs an over respectively. Then, after a promising opening partnership, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull, Tom Banton flicked straight to midwicket and Will Jacks later fell in identical fashion when well-set to marshal the chase. Arafat Minhas ended up with six for 40, bowling Harry Brook with a beauty, and there will be more trial by spin today.

Although there was some talk of England failing in end-of-days Bazball fashion, it most reminded me of the teething troubles of Eoin Morgan’s side in 2015 and 2016 when they were experimenting with players, viz this Rose Bowl collapse. We have to acknowledge that Joe Root, the best player of spin, was undone by one that kept low from Naseem Shah and both Brook and Jordan Cox lost their wickets to very good deliveries from Arafat, a bowler, on a feast day. Dunith Welllalage will return to try to replicate his line of attack today but he is a bowler that England know well. He has had his days against them but they have also given him some tap in the past.
