World.title: Malawi: Schools Urged to Adapt As Heatwave Warning Issued Across Malawi
World.content:
Schools and other learning institutions have been urged to implement immediate measures to protect learners and staff following a heatwave alert issued by the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS).

The Department has forecast temperatures of up to 42C in parts of the Southern Region, with unusually high temperatures also expected across the Central, Northern and lakeshore areas.

In a statement, Secretary for Education Dr Ken Ndala said institutions should strictly adhere to precautionary measures aimed at safeguarding learners, teachers and support staff while maintaining continuity in education.

Schools have been advised to adjust timetables, relax uniform requirements and adopt flexible learning arrangements where necessary to reduce exposure to extreme heat.



The ministry has also directed institutions to suspend or reschedule outdoor activities, including sports, assemblies, parades and manual work, during the hottest part of the day, between 10am and 3pm.

Additional guidance includes ensuring continuous access to safe drinking water, encouraging regular hydration, keeping classrooms cool and well-ventilated, making use of shaded areas and avoiding overcrowding.

Schools have also been asked to pay particular attention to vulnerable groups, including young children, people with albinism, pregnant members of staff and those living with chronic health conditions.

"The ministry also reminds institutions to make use of the El Niño Practical Guidance for the Education Sector 2026-2027 booklets that have been distributed to strengthen preparedness and response to climate-related hazards," the statement said.

The advisory forms part of wider efforts to minimise the impact of extreme weather conditions on learning and to reduce health risks associated with prolonged exposure to high temperatures.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 23, 2026
World.content:
Tanzania Opposition Official Charged With Treason

A senior official of Tanzania's main opposition party, Chadema, John Pambalu, has been charged with treason, an offence that carries a potential death penalty. Pambalu, a member of the party's national council and former youth wing leader, is accused of seeking to disrupt the 2025 general election through protests intended to intimidate the government. He is the second senior Chadema figure to face treason charges after party leader Tundu Lissu. The charges come amid a wider crackdown on government critics following the October 2025 elections, which President Samia Suluhu Hassan officially won with 98% of the vote. Opposition groups and rights organisations say about 2,000 people were killed during the subsequent protests. A government-initiated inquiry put the death toll at 518. Chadema was excluded from the election, and party officials have vowed to continue challenging the government.

Immigrant Beaten to Death in Durban, South Africa

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, prompting a police investigation amid growing anti-immigrant tensions in South Africa. Police said the unidentified man was believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s. He was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The motive remains unclear. The killing follows a series of anti-immigrant protests that have turned violent in parts of the country, with shops and vehicles set alight in Durban and Soweto. Several African countries, including Nigeria, Ghana and Zimbabwe, have expressed concern over attacks on their citizens, with some arranging repatriations. South Africa has experienced xenophobic violence for nearly two decades, including deadly attacks in 2008 that killed more than 60 people. The unrest is unfolding amid widespread unemployment, poverty and inequality. Researchers said broad claims that migrants cause crime and job losses are not supported by evidence.

Malawi Opposition Demands Answers Over President's Absence

Malawi's opposition Malawi Congress Party has demanded answers over President Peter Mutharika's prolonged absence from the country while the nation faces fuel shortages, medicine scarcity and rising living costs. Campaign director Moses Kunkuyu said the concern was not the president's private trip abroad but the government's failure to communicate clearly about who was leading the country and responding to the crises. Motorists are spending hours waiting for fuel, while patients struggle to access essential medicines. The opposition also criticised Vice-President Jane Ansah for remaining silent, urging her to reassure citizens that the government is functioning and has a plan to address the shortages. The criticism comes as economic hardship deepens and public frustration grows over the lack of clear communication and action from the authorities.

Ruto Urges Africa to Finance Its Own Growth

Kenyan President William Ruto has urged African governments to strengthen and rely more on the continent's financial institutions to fund development. He said that Africa must take greater responsibility for its economic future. Speaking at the 25th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) summit in Harare, Zimbabwe, Ruto said Africa holds more than US$4 trillion in domestic financial assets, much of which remains in foreign accounts while local projects struggle to secure funding. He called on governments to invest their reserves in African institutions, support their bonds and guarantees, and channel more development projects through them. Ruto also urged countries to deepen regional trade, remove trade barriers and build stronger value chains as global protectionism increases. He cited Kenya's investment in African financial institutions and said a planned US$16 billion East African refinery in Kenya would be financed almost entirely by African institutions. Ruto handed over COMESA's chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa, stressing that regional integration must deliver tangible benefits for citizens.

Africa CDC Warns No Country Is Safe as Ebola Spreads to Nigeria

The Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus has killed 4,690 people and remains uncontrolled, with Nigeria reporting its first case in more than a decade, according to Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention director-general Jean Kaseya. The outbreak, which began in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May, has recorded 9,735 confirmed cases, with eight provinces in the country affected and an estimated 65 to 70 new cases reported daily. The Nigerian patient, a woman who arrived in Abuja on October 3, was diagnosed 16 days later, raising concerns about possible exposure to numerous contacts. The World Health Organization said 44 contacts had been identified and were being monitored, while authorities investigate where she contracted the virus. Kaseya stressed the need for stronger surveillance in hospitals, health facilities and across borders, amid conflicting accounts from Nigerian and Ugandan officials about the woman's travel history. There is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus. Kaseya also defended calls for greater transparency in the management of international Ebola response funding, saying governments need clear information about resources entering their countries.

Close 

Mali Army, Russian-Linked Forces Accused of Civilian Abuses

Human Rights Watch has accused Mali's armed forces and Russia-controlled Africa Corps of committing serious abuses against civilians in the central Mopti region during renewed fighting. The organisation said an apparent military drone strike on September 16 killed eight civilians and injured at least six others in Guélédié village. Witnesses reported that the strike hit an area where residents had gathered to access satellite internet, although armed fighters linked to al-Qaeda were reportedly present in the village. Human Rights Watch also documented alleged torture and inhumane detention at a military base in Sévaré between May and August, where civilians were reportedly held in overcrowded shipping containers without adequate food, water, sanitation or medical care. Former detainees described severe beatings, electric shocks and waterboarding, and alleged that several prisoners died while in custody. The Malian military said its September operation targeted suspected militants and destroyed their equipment. Human Rights Watch called for credible investigations and accountability, warning that attacks on civilians, torture and denial of medical care may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and, in some cases, war crimes.

World.title: Tanzania: Top Tanzanian Opposition Figure John Pambalu Charged With Treason
World.content:
A senior official of Tanzania's main opposition party, Chadema, John Pambalu, has been charged with treason, an offence that carries a potential death penalty.

Pambalu, a member of the party's national council and former youth wing leader, is accused of seeking to disrupt the 2025 general election through protests intended to intimidate the government.

He is the second senior Chadema figure to face treason charges after party leader Tundu Lissu.

The charges come amid a wider crackdown on government critics following the October 2025 elections, which President Samia Suluhu Hassan officially won with 98% of the vote. Opposition groups and rights organisations say about 2,000 people were killed during the subsequent protests.

A government-initiated inquiry put the death toll at 518. Chadema was excluded from the election, and party officials have vowed to continue challenging the government.

World.title: ESPN posts propagandistic headline about Trump, LeBron and national anthem
World.content:
NBA star LeBron James was shown practicing his golf swing during the playing of the United States national anthem before his 76ers debut on Tuesday. Later in the week, President Donald Trump called James' conduct a "TOTAL DISGRACE" on social media.

The story itself is quite simple. James practiced his golf swing during "The Star-Spangled Banner." Trump criticized him for it. And yet, the headline writers at ESPN apparently didn't see it quite as clearly.

According to ESPN.com on Thursday, "Trump criticizes LeBron James for not standing still during the national anthem."

Take a look:

Here's the full clip of James during the national anthem:

Describing what James did as merely "not standing still" is an awfully charitable characterization. He wasn't shifting his feet or adjusting his uniform. He was practicing his golf swing while the national anthem played.

The framing minimizes the conduct at the center of the controversy. ESPN suggested James' behavior was innocuous and Trump's criticism was excessive.

That was the point. ESPN must feel it has an obligation to protect James. The headline writers must have also agreed James was wrong. Otherwise, there would be no reason to sanitize it as James merely failing to "stand still."

At least athletes who kneel during the anthem generally claim that they are doing so as a form of protest. James offered no such explanation. He simply sought to make a mockery of the anthem.

It also wasn't the first time. James was caught practicing his swing during the national anthem on Christmas Day last year.

There’s something cringe about a star American athlete who previously criticized NBA executive Daryl Morey for supporting Hong Kong protesters now behaving this way during the U.S. national anthem.

At this stage of his career, the NBA also has to ask how much James still benefits its brand.

James turns 42 in December. He has averaged 15 points per game through his first two games this season and, unsurprisingly at his age, is a shell of his former self.

His basketball legacy is secure. James is one of the greatest players in NBA history. But he has become a net negative through his declining play and consistently anti-American messaging.

World.title: Vance receives warm reception during Bengals visit despite negative media portrayal: source
World.content:
The narrative on social media that Vice President JD Vance was ignored by multiple Cincinnati Bengals players at a recent team practice apparently does not reflect what actually unfolded that day, a source with knowledge of the visit told OutKick.

A recent video shared online showed Vance and his family outside the team's locker room on Thursday as the team walked back in. The video, that did not have clear audio of the interaction, showed Bengals tight end Drew Sample stop to shake the vice president's hand as other players walked by.

But footage obtained by OutKick portrayed a different story, including a handshake with an enthusiastic Bengals head coach Zac Taylor. The video also captured audio and appeared to show Vance chopping it up with players and other staffers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Seeing how the media works is actually pretty crazy. The players, staff, and Vice President Vance and his son all had a great time at practice," the source told OutKick exclusively. "All of these negative tweets and articles are completely detached from the reality of how well the visit went."

Initial reaction to the video shared on social described the interaction as Vance getting "snubbed" by the team.

"This is what TOTAL HUMILIATION looks like: JD Vance attempted to greet Cincinnati Bengals players in the locker room and got snubbed and ghosted by every single player except one," one person wrote on X.

"JD Vance walked into the Bengals locker room looking for a photo-op, and the players gave him the cold shoulder he deserves," another person wrote, adding that the team didn't want to be used for"political theater."

But the source told OutKick that Vance and his son were warmly received when visiting the facility with no planned media engagement. A photo obtained by OutKick showed the vice president and his family playing catch on the field. The source added that defensive lineman Dexter Lawrence approached the vice president and had conversation with him during the visit.

TITANS PLAYER WHO GOT INTO ARGUMENT THAT PROVOKED 'UNFORTUNATE' GUN INCIDENT SPEAKS OUT

Vance, an Ohio native, is a longtime Bengals fan, growing up roughly an hour outside of Cincinnati. He has a home in Cincinnati’s East Walnut Hills neighborhood.

Vance toured the team's locker room, shook hands with several players, coach Zac Taylor and others, and came away with a football. It is unclear if Vance brought the ball to be autographed or the club gave it to him as a memento.

Quarterback Joe Burrow said he "did not" talk to Vance.

"He came with everybody and left with swiftness and efficiency before the end of practice, so I didn't get to," Burrow told reporters earlier this week.



Vance was in town to deliver a speech at the FBI's Cincinnati Field Office and then hold a campaign rally at the Sharonville Convention Center.

OutKick's Armando Salguero contributed to this report.

World.title: Colorado high school volleyball players faced alleged benching threat amid trans athlete dispute
World.content:
Two Colorado high school volleyball players were threatened with benching after discussing a transgender athlete in their program, according to a parent complaint alleging the girls were ultimately allowed to play on condition they stop discussing the issue. The school district that oversees the school, Jefferson County Schools, is currently under Title IX investigation by the U.S. Department of Education.

A screenshot of an email, obtained by OutKick, from Dakota Ridge High School's head volleyball coach to a parent says the parent's daughter would miss a match over reports of alleged bullying. The screenshot does not identify the actual words that were used.

"Over the past several days, we have received multiple reports alleging that your daughter used language toward teammates that could be characterized as bullying," the message bearing the coach's name states.

"As a result, your daughter will not be eligible to participate in today’s match."

EX-SJSU VOLLEYBALL COACH FILES NEW LAWSUIT ALLEGING RETALIATION FOR TRUMP SUPPORT, RELIGION AMID TRANS SCANDAL

The message says the volleyball program emphasizes character, respect and how players treat one another, describing the reported behavior as falling short of its standards. It offers to discuss the matter with the parent after the match.

Meanwhile, Tanna Donalson, whose daughter was cut from the program in August, wrote in an Oct. 6 email to district that her daughter had reported two varsity players were told they would be benched after discussing the situation among friends. Donalson said she was subsequently informed that, after the players’ parents met with the coach and the athletic director, the girls were permitted to play on condition they not discuss the issue again.

The email was seen by OutKick in a copy of a Title IX complaint Donalson submitted to the Education Department.

"[The daughter] reported that Mr. Zeman pulled three varsity volleyball players aside and told two of them they would be benched for today’s game because they had discussed this issue amongst themselves. According to the account relayed to me, four friends had been discussing privately what they had learned, and one reported the conversation to a teacher. I was further informed that, after the two players’ parents met with the athletic director and Mr. Zeman, the players were permitted to play on the condition that they not discuss the issue again," Donalson wrote.

"Please determine what was said, the basis for the proposed benching, and whether participation was conditioned on refraining from discussion of or support for our complaint."

Lindsay Datko, founder of the parent advocacy group Jeffco Kids First, also said she had reviewed emails concerning the threatened discipline.

"We have seen emails showing that girls were threatened to be benched because they were expressing their frustration in a very adolescent manner," Datko told OutKick.

But Datko added the coach backed away from the threatened benching.

EDUCATION DEPARTMENT RESCINDS BIDEN TITLE IX RULE, RESTORES TRUMP-ERA REGULATIONS

Jeffco Chief Legal Counsel Julie Tolleson acknowledged Donalson’s report in an Oct. 6 email response.

"She can include these matters in her review, though we won’t be able to discuss with you any disciplinary or other action involving any other student," Tolleson wrote, referring to the district’s Title IX coordinator.

A day earlier, Tolleson had instructed Donalson to report any retaliation or harassment related to her complaint.

"District policy prohibits retaliation," she wrote.

In response to OutKick, Jeffco defended its policies and cited student privacy restrictions. Its statement did not address the alleged condition on the players’ participation or explain what remarks prompted the proposed discipline.

The school district provided the following response in full:

"We recognize that fairness in athletics, student safety, privacy, and equitable opportunities for students are important issues for our community.

"In accordance with Colorado state law (including the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act), Jeffco Public Schools is committed to providing a safe, welcoming, and inclusive environment for all students. Jeffco’s policies ensure that every student, regardless of gender identity or expression, has equal access to educational programs, facilities, and district-sanctioned activities.

"High School Athletics: Jeffco Public Schools operates high school athletic programs under the governing bylaws of the Colorado High School Activities Association (CHSAA) and Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act.

"District Policies on Equal Educational Opportunities Jeffco Public Schools' nondiscrimination policies—including Policy AC (Nondiscrimination/Equal Opportunity) and related guidance—remain fully active and in effect.

"Under federal law (FERPA) and state privacy regulations, Jeffco Public Schools cannot confirm, deny, or comment on the gender identity, administrative records, or athletic participation of any individual student.

"We are navigating a complex national climate, but our local commitment remains steady: all students deserve to feel safe, respected, and supported in Jeffco Public Schools. We support and value all members of our Jeffco community, including our transgender students and staff members.

"Jeffco Public Schools is committed to cultivating environments where all students, staff, families, and members of our community are accepted, respected, and feel that their voices and perspectives are valued. While people may have differing views on Jeffco policies and the laws that inform them, we all share a responsibility to ensure our words and actions reflect care and respect for others. We ask everyone in our community to respect individual privacy and remember that real children and families are at the heart of these conversations.

"Jeffco will continue to follow all state laws and regulations with respect to our schools, athletic programs, and students’ rights. Our responsibility - and steadfast commitment - remains to serve every student and ensure that our schools are places where all students can learn, grow, and thrive."

Donalson’s own complaint centers on the roster decision that ended her daughter's junior-year school volleyball season.

Her daughter, 17, had played in the program during her freshman and sophomore years. Her mother said coaches encouraged the setter to learn right-side hitting before ultimately cutting her.

In an Aug. 13 email, the coach said the change was intended to give her daughter another opportunity to demonstrate her skills. He said other athletes showed greater consistency in setting, defense, serving, decision-making and other areas, and described the roster decisions as a collective coaching evaluation.

WASHINGTON STATE'S HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS LEAGUE PUTS ONUS FOR TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY ON STATE LAWS

"She competed for a spot, other athletes ultimately demonstrated more consistency in the areas needed, and she was beat out," he wrote.

The coach is also her daughter's history teacher. Correspondence documents Donalson’s request for a different placement and the school’s offer of a teacher change for second semester. Donalson responded that she wanted to give the situation a few weeks before deciding. She explicitly told school officials she was not alleging that classroom retaliation had occurred.

Asked whether her family had experienced retaliation since speaking publicly, she said she had reported that some students made comments to her daughter, but their family had received substantially more support than opposition.

"We have received far more support than we have anything opposite of that," she said.

The U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights issued findings March 13 that the district violated Title IX through its policies on girls’ athletics and access to female facilities and overnight accommodations. OCR issued a notice of impending enforcement action June 26. Jeffco disputes those findings.

The district sued Education Secretary Linda McMahon and the Education Department on July 28, challenging the enforcement actions and arguing that the federal demands conflict with Colorado law and threaten its funding. That lawsuit concerns the district’s broader policies, rather than a determination about Donalson's daughter's roster decision.

Colorado voters will consider Proposition 134 on Nov. 3. The measure would require school-based teams to be designated for biological males, biological females or mixed participation, with eligibility tied to those categories and an exception allowing females to join male teams when no equivalent female team is offered.

"I am not against the trans community or any community for that matter," Donalson said when asked about the measure.

For Donalson and her daughter, she says the impact of the situation has been "deep and wide," and has jeopardized her daughter's dreams of playing in college.

"She still has those dreams, it's a little difficult to figure out how we're going to achieve them, as this is her junior year, and arguably her most important year, because that is when you start communicating with coaches," Donalson said. "And right now we have nothing to share."

She said her daughter still plans to play club volleyball and pursue college opportunities. But losing her school season has affected how she experiences the sport.

"Every time she plays, she just remembers all that’s transpired here, and it just has taken a little bit of the joy of the sport out of it for her," Donalson said.

World.title: Irish politicians disavow ‘demeaning’ PSA warning grandparents not to hug family without asking consent

An ad released by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) in Ireland that urged grandparents to ask for consent before hugging their grandchildren sparked international controversy after it began airing last month and has since been removed.

In September, an ad from the DRCC’s We-Consent campaign went viral for showing grandparents greeting their grandchildren. One grandchild appears receptive to a hug, while the other does not. A narrator says, "Not everyone wants a hug, even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."

The ad has since been removed and criticized by politicians from multiple parties in Ireland.

The BBC reported that Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan of the Fianna Fáil party, whose department funded the campaign, announced the video has been removed after discussion with the DRCC, and declared, it "does not represent the views of the Government."

IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND 'NOT OVERRUN' BY MIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS

"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them," O'Callaghan said. "While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."

Irish Sen. Gareth Scahill of the Fine Gael party blasted the video as a waste of public funds.

"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which, at best, has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," Scahill said.

"The issue of consent is a very serious one, and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children.

"But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark."

TRUMP SAYS HE WOULD 'LOVE' TO SEE IRELAND UNIFIED AS ONE NATION

Scahill also asked, "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"

The DRCC told Irish broadcaster RTE in a statement, "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.

"We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too," the organization added. "We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have."

"Instead of honestly acknowledging what is behind the doubling of rape rates from a decade ago, which is who the government chooses to let into the country, these institutions lecture grandparents about hugging their grandkids, as though that has any remotest connection to the problem at hand," she said.

World.title: DOJ sues to block Alaska Senate certification if GOP’s Dan Sullivan loses
World.content:
The Justice Department has filed suit against Alaska election officials, seeking to block the results of November’s U.S. Senate election from being certified unless incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan wins — a controversial move President Donald Trump claimed credit for.

In papers filed in federal court, attorneys for the DOJ argued the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot could mislead supporters of the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan.

“For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan,” the filing says.

“To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the suit says.

The Trump administration is seeking a court order blocking the results from being certified “if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

Trump told reporters Friday that he directed the suit to be filed.

“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump said, calling Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy “a disgrace.”

The filing by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the action was brought “to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.”

Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee in the Senate race, blasted the move in a post on X, saying, “This is the corruption AK is fed up with,” and that Sullivan is “using his DC allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans.”

Sullivan’s Senate office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit, nor did his campaign when asked about the suit and Peltola’s post.

Alaska’s Division of Elections said in a statement that it is reviewing the complaint and is “focused on running the ongoing election and giving voter’s confidence that their votes will count.”

“This also includes assisting voters and avoiding voter confusion — whether through the information in the Official Election Pamphlet, asking questions of a poll worker, or bringing others to assist you with voting as permitted by law,” the department said.

The Trump administration filed the suit Thursday, the same day Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that “it is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.”

“I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said, although there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which DOJ would seek to get involved.

It’s unclear why the department decided to seek action now, with Election Day less than two weeks away.

U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results.

The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, which chiefly allows the department to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law.

While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said there’s no law that says DOJ can challenge ballots or delay certification.

A DOJ spokesperson told NBC News in a statement that Sullivan’s “candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot. Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”

A DOJ official called the situation “unique.”

David Becker, executive director for the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the legal action “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government” in a statement.

“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” he said, and the “DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy.”

Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy has already been challenged in Alaska, where in August he finished in third place with 2.5% of the vote in the all-party primary. Peltola received 49.5% and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%.

Sullivan Jr. was initially booted from the ballot in June after election officials found his candidacy was not in “good faith,” citing his choice to run using the name Dan instead of Daniel and being “affiliated with the Republican Party” when he had previously “never — according to the Division’s records — been affiliated with the Republican Party in Alaska.”

The Alaska courts, however, ruled he could stay on the ballot.

The November ballot does differentiate the two Sullivans. “Dan S. Sullivan” is listed with a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while the other is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation next to his name.

Sullivan Jr. did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Sullivan’s campaign and his Republican allies have charged Sullivan Jr. is a Democratic dupe, being used to draw votes away from the incumbent. Trump has repeatedly criticized Sullivan Jr. as a “cheat.”

“It’s cheating. It’s a spoiler candidate to go on the ballot with the exact same name as your great Senator Dan Sullivan. This guy’s name is Dan Sullivan. He knew nothing about politics. He was just put there by the Democrats to confuse the voter, and it’s very unfair. But that’s what they do. They cheat. They lie. They steal,” Trump said in a video post on social media earlier this month.

NBC News reported back in July that federal and state investigators were looking at whether Sullivan Jr. could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters, citing two people with knowledge of the matter. The status of that investigation is unclear.

A spokesperson for Peltola said earlier this year that her “campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”

Sullivan Jr., a former teacher, told The Associated Press back in June that his candidacy is no sham and that he’s not in cahoots with anybody.

“I have every right to run for whatever office I’m qualified for, and I’m qualified for this office,” he said then. “I think I’m doing what most Americans would think would be a patriotic thing to do when you’re unsatisfied with the status quo. You stand up and say, ‘I’m going to fight for things I believe that are going to make my community better.’”

World.title: Trump administration cancels some Canada tariffs amid close midterm races
World.content:
The Trump administration on Friday said it had granted tariff exemptions on some Canadian imports, an implicit acknowledgement that President Donald Trump’s signature trade policy could be hurting Republican candidates running in the Nov. 3 midterm election.

The canceled tariffs include 50% duties on some agricultural items. These duties were applied to Canadian products after the country withdrew from trade negotiations with the Trump administration in late August.

Polls show Democrats have a solid chance to win majorities in both the House and Senate.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who’s facing a tough re-election battle in Maine, first announced the news on social media: “I am pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.”

She said that plastic boxes, crates, packing materials, refrigeration equipment, sealing and labeling machinery, packing equipment, film, foil and seaweed products were some of the other products getting exemptions.

A document posted to the White House website confirmed the action, but it said that the administration was also adding tariffs to “certain valves, carpets, waste products” and other items to make up for the duties it was removing.

The White House statement said the move aimed to “further refine the scope of the tariffs” applied to Canada.

Collins, in her announcement, said that many “farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”

Democrat Troy Jackson, who is challenging Collins for her Senate seat, responded by saying: “Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”

He added on X: “Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving.”

Collins’ announcement did not mention Trump, only top administration officials such as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The White House announcement made no mention of Collins, who has occasionally sparred with Trump.

“I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” Collins said.

The Commerce Department and Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Other Republicans have broken with Trump’s most well-known economic policy, too. Mike Rogers, who’s in a tight race for a Senate seat in Michigan, told NBC News last week that he would like to see the trade war with Canada “wrapped up.”

After U.S. officials made what Prime Minister Mark Carney called “unfair” and “uneconomic” demands, the U.S. hit Canada with two waves of tariffs, the second of which included the 50% duties.

Trump has repeatedly said “there’s nothing they have that we need” from Canada. “We have everything,” Trump said in September.

On Sept. 28, Trump predicted that Carney would be removing tariffs. “I think what’s going to happen is over the next three or four weeks, they’re going to come to us, and they’re going to say, ‘we’re going to get rid of all the tariffs,’” the president said.

“We’re going to win everything,” Trump predicted. “They’re going to come in, and they’re going to say, ‘Sir, we are sorry.’”

Asked about Trump’s prediction a day later, Carney laughed during a press conference, adding that he had no additional comment to make.

Carney has stood steady in the face of repeated verbal attacks from Trump since the trade war kicked off in August. As Trump has ramped up social media attacks, Carney has turned to the rest of the world, opening up Canada’s economy to China, India, and the United Kingdom.

Next week, Carney is set to reach a historic agreement with the European Union over the terms of becoming the bloc’s first-ever “associate member” during an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal.

The European Union’s 27 member states collectively are the world’s single largest trading bloc and the union is the world’s third largest behind the U.S. and China.

World.title: Trump doubles down on defending Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton
World.content:
President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his support of a widely condemned attack ad against Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, saying that he won’t change his mind about the $4 million ad campaign by her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, that features her estranged mother calling her a “liar.”

Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if he has changed his mind about defending the minutelong ad, now that he knows the backstory about Acton’s late stepfather, whom Acton has said sexually abused her as a child.

“No, it’s a mother speaking badly against Amy Acton,” Trump said. “If it were my mother speaking badly about me, you’d be making it the No. 1 story on the news.”

Trump also criticized an NBC News reporter who pressed him further about the situation, calling her “a fresh person” and “horrible little reporter.”

Asked by NBC News about Republicans who have denounced the ad, Trump said “They don’t know the facts.”

“A mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there, because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar.’ Why shouldn’t somebody use that?” he added.

The president first voiced support for the ad in a post on Truth Social Thursday, suggesting that Republicans were being treated unfairly. “If my mother, the legendary Mary MacLeod Trump, said anything bad about me, the Fake News would play it up,” Trump wrote. “The Dumocrats would be totally supportive, and it would go down as the Ad of the Decade — Maybe the Century!”

He then addressed the controversy in remarks at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa at night, claiming that Ramaswamy asked him what to do amid the media firestorm.

“I said, ‘You got to ride with it,’” Trump recounted.

Ramaswamy defended the ad at a campaign bus tour stop in Strongsville, Ohio, Friday morning. He accused the “flawed and failed media” of “lying about an ad that is about lying.” His campaign told NBC News on Thursday that it planned a $4 million push to air the ad.

“It had nothing to do with childhood abuse, which I will be the No. 1 governor to prosecute when I am the governor of this state, because it is wrong and we together will fight against that across Ohio. That is the truth — that they’re changing the subject because they don’t want to answer for their own failures,” Ramaswamy told a crowd of supporters.

Documents obtained by NBC News from the Mahoning County Clerk of Courts show Acton’s stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and indicted by a grand jury in 1978 in Ohio for rape involving a child under 13 years old between 1976 and 1978. While the victim’s name is redacted in the records, Acton’s biological father, Gerald Stearns, signed one of the documents.

Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton said she has not spoken to her mother since the 1978 trial. Joshua A. Bickel / Columbus Dispatch via USA Today

At the White House, a reporter noted that Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, stood by the stepfather during the trial. “Look, you don’t know that,” Trump said. “You don’t know anything.”

Acton has said she has not seen or spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years. Arthur has not responded to requests for comment.

“Her mother went on television and said that the daughter who’s running for governor of Ohio is a liar and a bad person, and that’s all I know,” Trump said.

Trump continued, “The press is embarrassing themselves. You’re trying to take a horrible situation for a Democrat and make it look better. The mother said really bad things about a person that wants to be the Democrat governor of Ohio. The mother said terrible things. Anybody seeing that would say, ‘No way, I’m voting for her.’”

Trump said that Acton’s mother looks “very lucid” and “very smart” in the ad. After the spot surfaced Monday, Acton’s campaign described it as an “attempt to platform” an “estranged and abusive mother.”

“If my mother said bad things about me, you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so. But my mother thought I was wonderful. Thank you, Mom,” Trump said. “This has nothing to do with the stepfather or anything else.”

While Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a number of Republicans have condemned it. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, rebuked it on Thursday, telling reporters, “The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling.” He called on Ramaswamy to take it down, but said he still supports the entire Republican ticket in Ohio, including Ramaswamy.

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who faces a competitive re-election race, also criticized it, saying he wouldn’t have run the ad. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has previously spoken about being a sexual assault victim, called it “the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.” And Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who also faces a tight general election race, condemned the ad.

““It’s terrible. I think about it as a mom and you think about your kids surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again. I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down,” she said in an interview with ABC News on Thursday.

During a campaign stop in Cincinnati on Wednesday, Vance responded to the backlash from within his party, telling them to “stop whining” about the ad and to focus on winning midterm elections.

“Politics is a tough business,” Vance said. “And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an  and go win the race in 13 days.”

World.title: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
World.content:
The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection.

“As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service.

The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.”

“Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added.

Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied.

World.title: Hero who stopped Bend school shooter haunted by encounter: ‘I didn’t save everybody’
World.content:
A string of innocuous choices made by an Oregon father brought him to the elementary school where he killed a mass shooter in an act he believed would be his last.

Police have credited the quick thinking and decisive action of Bend carpenter Kaylub Giamanco for confronting 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and stopping the teen shooter’s carnage on Oct. 15.

The gunman had already killed a teacher and three young children at Silver Rail Elementary School and could have continued his attack had Giamanco, 36, not randomly ended up at the crime scene.

In an emotional and harrowing interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting published on Friday, Giamanco recalled that fateful day.

“I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small. I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family,” he told OPB. “I feel like if I’m going to have a voice, then I’ll be damned if I’m not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place.”

Giamanco’s presence in the neighborhood near Silver Rail came after a series of seemingly benign decisions the carpenter made that Thursday about lunch.

Giamanco packed a midday snack but changed his mind about eating it, instead opting to drive home to have leftover tacos with his wife, he said.

And on his way home, Giamanco had briefly considered going to a masonry shop to buy some bolts he needed, but again opted to go home for the tacos.

Police tape blocks access to Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 16. Payton Bruni / AFP via Getty

Those choices led him to Brentwood Avenue near his children’s school just before 1 p.m., where he spotted a “man in black” with a long gun opening fire on a motorist and a woman mowing the school lawn, he recalled.

Giamanco, who kept a .40 caliber handgun in his truck console, saw the killer toss his weapon over the school fence before climbing it himself.

The father understood what was happening and “that’s when panic filled into my brain, and that’s when I opened my center console.”

Giamanco, who has two girls, 5 and 10, attending Silver Rail, called 911 but couldn’t answer all of the dispatcher’s questions.

“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” said Giamanco.

As Giamanco got closer to the school building, he kept a low profile and from his knees could hear the bloodshed.

“That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself, ‘This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,’” he said.

Giamanco crawled in through a shot-out window, reached the special education classroom and reracked his firearm in preparation for a deadly confrontation.

He came upon the gunman and a teacher fighting for the killer’s gun.

“I knew that he did not know that I was there,” Giamanco said. “And I fired.”

The teacher fled, possibly believing Giamanco was a second attacker, he said. But the shooter was still alive and reaching for his gun.

“He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.”

Police arrived shortly after and Giamanco pleaded with them to let him call his loved ones.

“I called my wife to tell her that I’m not coming home for tacos,” he said.

Then he called his mother.

“She was just like, ‘OK, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You’re a hero. You saved lives.’ And I was just like, “I didn’t save everybody. I didn’t get them all.’”

Law enforcement officials have universally praised Giamanco for acting fast. Within hours of the shooting, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said of Giamanco and the teacher who fought with the killer: “I don’t think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage.”

Giamanco said he’s been struggling to sleep since the mass shooting and can’t get that terrible day out of his head.

“I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams,” he said.

The carpenter has not yet met the parents of the three children killed. Giamanco said he wants to tell them he’s sorry for not doing more.

“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco said, his voice choking with emotion. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”

World.title: House hunter discovers body in vacant home
World.content:
Florida resident David Hammersley and his family were fleeing from the hurricanes that plagued Florida and decided to tour homes in Kentucky. While house hunting on Sept. 26, 2022, their realtor showed them a rural 2-acre lot with a main house, a detached garage, and a cottage in Burkesville, Kentucky — a town known as the fishing capital of Kentucky.

"The house was immaculate. No furnishings in it. You can eat off the floor," Hammersley told correspondent Peter Van Sant in "The Mansion Above Dale Hollow Lake," an all-new "48 Hours" airing Saturday at 10/9c on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.

Hammersley was impressed with the property, including the sight of a Dodge truck found inside the detached garage.

"And I started to salivate over the possibility of that being part of the deal," he said.

The cottage, right, on the Kentucky property that became a crime scene. CBS News

As Hammersley and his family approached the cottage at the far end of the property, they were overpowered by a stench radiating from the cottage.

"It had to be something like a dead raccoon, in my opinion," Hammersley said.

Hammersley and his father-in-law proceeded to investigate, and within moments they stumbled across a horrific scene.

"I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched, obviously dead, from gunshot wounds," Hammersley told Van Sant.

They immediately contacted the authorities, who identified that man as Michael "Mike" Harding, a California transplant who resided across the Kentucky border in Tennessee. He had been missing for over a week.

An autopsy revealed that Harding had been shot four times — twice in the head and twice in the torso. Authorities found his phone at the crime scene and lead investigator BJ Burton from the Kentucky State Police examined it to see if it could answer their questions.

"Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls, it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house," Burton told Van Sant.

Investigators learned Harding had been contacted by a realtor named James Fraser requesting a repair service because Harding worked as an HVAC technician. However, they discovered the number used to contact Harding came from a prepaid cellphone.

"It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone," Burton said.

Burton also discovered Harding was going through a contentious divorce with his wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol. The two were living in separate places — he was in Tennessee and she was in California.

"I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her ... So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her," Mike Harding's daughter, Heather Cavalieri, told "48 Hours."

Mike and Julie Harding Preston and Crystal Cleary/Cumberland County Justice Center/CHP

Friends and family of Mike Harding told authorities he feared Julie Harding. They got access to her call log and learned that in the months leading up to his murder, Julie Harding had around 194 calls with a man from Houston. His name was Thomas O'Donnell and he was a former car salesman now living in Napa, California.

They also determined that the prepaid phone and O'Donnell's phone were located together a few weeks before Mike Harding's death.

"And the first thing you notice is ... the phone is first turned on when it's in the Houston, Texas, area," Burton said. "I don't think Mr. O'Donnell got out here by accident. The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding."

On Dec. 8, 2022, just two months after Mike Harding was found dead, authorities arrested O'Donnell for his murder. For Julie Harding, two days after O'Donnell's arrest, she was found dead at the Tennessee home where Mike Harding had been living. An investigator determined she had died by suicide.

Burton believes Julie Harding may have feared she would lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in their divorce, so she conspired with O'Donnell to kill her estranged husband. O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge and would face trial three years after his arrest. A Kentucky jury found him guilty, and he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.

World.title: Judge allows Jane Doe anonymity in Cornell sexual assault lawsuit
World.content:
A judge ruled Friday that Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit alleging sexual assault involving seven former members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity, can remain anonymous as the legal proceedings move forward.

Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond granted the anonymity protections, citing the highly publicized nature of the allegations, concerns about retaliation and threats and the potential harm that could result from publicly identifying the plaintiff.

In her ruling, the judge also suggested that the anonymity designation "should likewise be extended" to the defendants, adding that she would welcome such a filing.

The ruling requires court filings to conceal Jane Doe's identity and other sensitive personal information. However, defendants will be permitted to privately share identifying information when necessary to investigate the allegations and prepare their defense, subject to confidentiality protections.

Perry-Bond also encouraged broader privacy protections for defendants and witnesses involved in the case.

In her ruling, the judge warned that anyone who engages in cyberstalking, harassment or threats against Jane Doe, the defendants or their attorneys could face criminal prosecution.

The decision does not address the merits of the sexual assault allegations or determine whether any of the defendants are liable. Instead, it establishes privacy protections for those involved as the civil lawsuit proceeds.

In a civil lawsuit, Jane Doe alleged she was drugged, gang-raped and sexually assaulted by seven men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. All seven have denied the allegations.
