Nadaraya explained that, at this stage, the court was not convinced of the need to obtain additional evidence, as the requested materials relied on the same opinion already included in the case file.

Georgian Dream representatives accused the opposition of attempting to delay the proceedings. According to Archil Gorduladze, the defendants were filing motions that had no legal basis or relevance to the case. Tornike Cheishvili argued that the parties were expressing the same arguments using different terminology and that their motions were virtually identical.

Meanwhile, outside the courtroom…

– Georgia’s Public Defender (ombudsman) has yet to submit a legal opinion (amicus curiae) to the Constitutional Court, despite Lelo calling on him to do so on 19 October. According to First Deputy Public Defender Tamar Gvaramadze, the ombudsman’s office is holding internal discussions and no decision has yet been made.

– Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili said it was unacceptable for international actors to make statements intended to put pressure on the court. He argued that such statements served harmful political purposes.

Reactions after the hearing

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, compared the proceedings to Franz Kafka’s novel The Trial, saying that no-one really knew who was being accused of what. Badri Japaridze also said that, by the end of the second day of hearings, none of the parties understood exactly what Georgian Dream was accusing them of.

Ana Tsitlidze, a representative of the United National Movement, accused the judges of behaving like Georgian Dream activists. According to Lelo representative Irakli Kupradze, the proposed ban would affect not only the parties but also nearly a million Georgian voters.

Ana Buchukuri, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, suggested that the third day of hearings would also begin with procedural motions. She argued that the court’s refusal to grant any of the motions indicated that a decision had already been made.

World.title: Should state have right to ban political parties? Tbilisi street poll – Video
World.content:
Ban on Georgian opposition

Should the state have the right to ban political parties? Tbilisi residents answered reporters’ questions.

Context

The Constitutional Court of Georgia began examining a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 21 October, seeking to ban five opposition parties.

The lawsuit was signed by 88 Georgian Dream MPs, who claim that the parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits the establishment and activities of political parties aiming to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order.

The proposed ban on opposition parties is no ordinary constitutional case. The court’s ruling could determine what kind of country Georgia ultimately becomes. The case has therefore attracted widespread attention.

How respondents reacted to the question

Most Tbilisi residents interviewed by reporters said that banning political parties was unacceptable in a country that claims to be a democracy. They stressed the importance of a multiparty system and people’s right to choose.

Many said the current developments reminded them of a slide towards dictatorship, drawing comparisons with Russia, North Korea and even the Soviet Union.

One respondent echoed claims made on Georgian pro-government propaganda channels that the opposition had attempted to set fire to parliament and stage a coup, and should therefore be banned.

Another respondent said that banning political parties could be open to discussion, but only if the process was fair and transparent.

Many passers-by declined to comment and tried to avoid appearing on camera. This was hardly surprising, given that people approached on the street generally tend to avoid politically sensitive questions.

World.title: Vanity Fair: Trump son-in-law received $750m from Azerbaijani bank
World.content:
Kushner’s links to Azerbaijani bank

Reports have emerged of hundreds of millions of dollars being transferred through Azerbaijan to a secret bank account that Jared Kushner, the son-in-law and former senior adviser to US President Donald Trump, allegedly had access to.

However, no evidence has been presented that the money belonged to the Azerbaijani state or that Azerbaijani authorities were involved in arranging these transactions.

The name of the Azerbaijani bank through which the transfers were allegedly made has also not been disclosed.

According to an investigation published in Vanity Fair, Dutch intelligence, while monitoring Kushner’s phone, discovered that a large sum of money had been transferred from an Azerbaijani bank to an account in the United Arab Emirates.

The claims were detailed in an article by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole, published on 22 October. The article is an excerpt from his new book, Princes and Thieves.

The investigation refers to a bank account holding approximately $750m, as well as an additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan. The author links these financial transactions to unofficial diplomatic negotiations involving the United States, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel.

How did Dutch intelligence gain access to Kushner’s phone?

According to Matthew Cole’s investigation, the Netherlands’ Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) gained access to data from Kushner’s phone in late 2017 through a hacker linked to Russian military intelligence.

Dutch intelligence officers initially discovered screenshots from Kushner’s iPhone on Russian military intelligence servers. Then, exploiting the same technical vulnerability, they were able to monitor activity on his phone screen in early 2018.

The intelligence officers’ attention was drawn to Kushner’s use of a bank account in the UAE. According to the investigation, hundreds of millions of dollars had previously been transferred to this account from an Azerbaijani bank.

Dutch intelligence initially suspected that the bank account from which the funds originated might have been linked to the Azerbaijani government. However, the article does not provide any banking documents confirming this connection.

$750m and possible intermediary role of Azerbaijani bank

The account, referred to in the investigation as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, one of the UAE’s largest banks.

According to the author, the Saudi and UAE leadership transferred around $750m into the account from 2017 onwards. The funds were allegedly intended to finance unofficial foreign policy initiatives.

The account did not legally belong to Kushner. It was held by Watani Al Emarat, a charitable organisation funded by the UAE government. However, according to the investigation, Kushner had signing authority over the account, allowing him to carry out certain banking transactions.

The section of the investigation concerning Azerbaijan focuses particularly on the mechanism used to transfer the funds.

According to Cole, all the funds deposited into the account monitored by Dutch intelligence arrived in US dollars from an Azerbaijani bank.

The author claims that some Azerbaijani banks acted as intermediaries in transferring large sums of money abroad. They accepted funds in Saudi riyals and UAE dirhams before transferring the equivalent amounts overseas in US dollars, charging a commission of 6–7%.

Under the arrangement described, a client would transfer funds in local currency to an Azerbaijani bank, which would then send the equivalent amount in US dollars to a recipient abroad from a separate internal account. The author notes that such transactions could make it more difficult to trace the original source of the funds.

Additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel

The investigation also describes a second major financial transaction allegedly carried out through Azerbaijan.

According to the author’s sources, by spring 2018, UAE leader Mohammed bin Zayed had transferred around $1bn to Israel through Azerbaijan, allegedly intended for Kushner.

The second account, referred to by Cole as Beta, was reportedly held at the Bank of Israel.

The article claims that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was to be informed of any potential transfers from this account. According to the author, former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman acted as an intermediary between Kushner and Netanyahu.

Friedman categorically denied these allegations. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client was unaware of the accounts in question, had no involvement with them and had not broken any laws.

Kushner’s financial ties have previously come under scrutiny

The new allegations come amid ongoing debate in the US over Kushner’s business ties with Gulf states.

In March 2026, US Senator Ron Wyden and House Representative Robert Garcia launched an investigation into Kushner’s continued efforts to raise funds from foreign governments for his investment firm while simultaneously engaging in diplomatic activities.

The members of Congress sought to establish whether investments received by Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, from Middle Eastern governments could have influenced his involvement in US foreign policy.

An investigation published by The New Yorker in September reported that Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund had invested $2bn in Kushner’s firm in 2021. The UAE and Qatar also invested in Affinity Partners.

These were separate financial arrangements, not directly linked to the alleged secret banking transactions of 2017–2018 described in the Vanity Fair article.

In addition, on 1 October, CNN published an investigation into investments made by Kushner’s firm in Israeli financial group Phoenix Financial. According to CNN’s analysis, Phoenix Financial had invested in at least nine companies supplying equipment to the Israeli military.

However, CNN said it had found no evidence that Kushner’s diplomatic decisions had directly influenced these investments. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client had not been involved in the companies’ investment decisions.

On 8 October, Kushner published a detailed response on his website to the earlier New Yorker article, rejecting allegations that he had used his diplomatic activities for personal financial gain.

Which previous investigations have implicated Azerbaijani banks?

Azerbaijan’s role in international financial transactions has previously been the subject of journalistic investigations.

In 2017, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), together with its partners, published a major investigation titled The Azerbaijani Laundromat.

The investigation documented financial transactions totalling around $2.9bn, carried out between 2012 and 2014 through various companies and bank accounts.

According to OCCRP, around $1.4bn of this amount was transferred through Baktelekom LLC, a company that held an account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan.

The investigation highlighted the role of Azerbaijan-linked financial entities in international money transfers. However, there is no confirmed link between this scheme and the recently reported accounts allegedly connected to Kushner.

Meanwhile, in January 2026, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Experts on the Evaluation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures and the Financing of Terrorism (MONEYVAL) reported progress by Azerbaijan in this area.

The committee upgraded Azerbaijan’s compliance ratings against international standards in seven areas, including money transfer controls, identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of legal entities and banking supervision.

However, the country remained subject to enhanced monitoring.

World.title: Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo continue to return to wild – video
World.content:
Nine red deer born at Tbilisi Zoo have returned to the wild — or, more precisely, to a semi-wild environment. They have moved to Algeti National Park, near Tbilisi.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: video

Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo were first moved to Algeti National Park in the summer of 2025. It was the first attempt to reintroduce the species into the wild in Georgia.

The process will continue in the coming years until the park has enough deer to restore the population.

The idea of restoring Georgia’s deer population emerged in the 1990s, when their numbers in the country fell sharply. Poaching and uncontrolled hunting contributed to the decline. Today, the red deer features on Georgia’s Red List of threatened species. In 2023, at the initiative of the Ministry of Environmental Protection and with funding from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency, authorities drew up a national plan to restore endangered species.

Zurab Gurielidze, a professor at Ilia State University and director of Tbilisi Zoo, led the development of the plan. As part of the project, authorities established an enclosed area of around 60 hectares in Algeti National Park, providing the deer with a suitable habitat and the conditions they need.

The process will take time and require continuous monitoring, adequate protection and cooperation between various agencies. Once the deer population in the park reaches a sufficient level, authorities will release the animals fully into the wild, where they will be able to live independently.

World.title: ‘Another attempt is being prepared to deprive Armenia of its independence’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence

“For the first time in our history, the ‘metropolis’ is not drawing us towards it. Instead, it seems to be saying, ‘We will push you away’,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said, commenting on a report on the possibility of suspending Armenia’s participation in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

Speaking at his weekly briefing, he stressed that the documents governing the EAEU do not give member states the authority to expel another member. The report makes the same point.

However, he drew a parallel with another organisation operating under Russia’s auspices: the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO).

“The CSTO allows for such a possibility. Since the EAEU and CSTO have essentially the same member states, the question arises: why don’t they expel Armenia from the CSTO?” Pashinyan asked.

According to the prime minister, the restrictions Russia has imposed on Armenia in recent months have failed to achieve the results that certain circles, both inside and outside the country, had hoped for. The measures include a ban on exporting most Armenian food products and other goods to Russia. Pashinyan said the move had failed to achieve either its economic or political objectives.

The prime minister sees Russia’s economic pressure as an attempt to trigger domestic political instability and deprive Armenia of its independence.

Journalists asked him to clarify whether Russia itself was destabilising Armenia.

“I said very specifically: certain circles in the Russian Federation — yes. Is that news to you?” he replied.

Nevertheless, Pashinyan said he was confident that Armenia was “resilient enough and would overcome this situation too”.

“Time will tell”: on the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council’s report

Armenian journalists asked Pashinyan what he thought about the risk of a catastrophic economic downturn if Armenia left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), as experts from the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council have forecast.

“Time will tell. Our main priority is Armenia’s continued development and the protection of our independence and sovereignty, as well as diversifying our relations. We will follow this path,” the prime minister replied.

In his view, forces both inside and outside Armenia are trying to exploit the current situation and problems in Armenia-Russia relations. Their aim, he said, is not only to trigger political instability in the country but also to effectively abolish Armenia’s independence.

The prime minister did not specify which forces he meant. However, he noted that several such attempts had taken place over the past three years. First, he recalled the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, particularly the exodus of the entire Armenian population from their homeland while Russian peacekeepers were present.

“The aim was to channel the flow of people into Armenia, while calls for a change of political power were coming from well-known quarters,” he said.

Pashinyan considers the situation surrounding the 2026 parliamentary elections to be a second attempt. He appears to be referring to hybrid attacks on Armenia and an alleged attempt to bring Armenians living in Russia to the polls to vote for pro-Russian forces.

“A third attempt is now being prepared. It is part of a certain ‘secret plan’ that is currently the subject of widespread discussion,” he concluded.

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition party Strong Armenia, has recently spoken openly about a “secret plan” to change the government. He has invoked the plan when asked what steps the opposition intends to take to overthrow the authorities after losing the election.

The prime minister believes the struggle is political rather than economic:

“The aim is to provoke domestic political instability in Armenia. As a consequence, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to deprive Armenia of its independence — first de facto, and then de jure.”

He added that events over the past several decades had also been directed towards achieving this goal.

“There will be no apocalypse”: on a possible rise in Russian gas prices

Pashinyan stressed that there was no guarantee that gas prices would remain unchanged. He also said that prices had risen at least twice over the past eight years.

“Gas prices have gone up before. You simply didn’t know about it. They rose in 2019 and then — I can’t remember exactly whether it was in 2022 or 2023. The point is that, thanks to citizens who work in Armenia, create added value and pay the taxes required by law, the Armenian government managed to ensure that the public did not notice these increases.”

The prime minister is convinced that even if gas prices rise by 69%, as the EAEU has warned, the Armenian economy will not face an “apocalypse”.

“Those who talk about an apocalypse simply don’t understand economics. I say that quite plainly.”

As the prime minister noted, people also predicted an “apocalypse” in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Yet Armenia’s economy grew throughout those years, Pashinyan said.

“You cannot erase history”: on relations with Russia

Speaking about his communications with Putin and Armenian-Russian relations, Pashinyan stressed that the relationship had always been positive and would remain so. However, he said this did not mean Armenia could simply erase the events of 2020, 2021 and 2023 from its history.

“That does not mean our history will no longer record the weapons we paid for but never received. Nor will it erase September 2022. That month, when Azerbaijani forces invaded Armenia’s sovereign territory, the CSTO failed to fulfil its treaty obligations to Armenia. This had extremely serious consequences.”

The prime minister’s conclusion was clear: dependence on a single country for weapons, gas and even apricots poses a threat to the state.

“We must address this threat. We are increasing Armenia’s level of independence. Are we doing so deliberately? Let’s put it this way — yes. We are consciously, you could even say relentlessly, strengthening the independence and sovereignty of the Republic of Armenia.”

Pashinyan concluded the discussion by saying that “the current situation is much more serious than many people think”. He said Armenia’s independence and statehood were at stake.

“We must learn the lessons of history,” he added.

Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence

World.title: Azerbaijan highlights hisability rights reforms and mine victims at the UN
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 24. Azerbaijan’s state policy on disability is based on the principles of inclusion, integration, equality, non-discrimination, and respect for the individual characteristics of persons with disabilities.

This was stated by Shahriyar Hajiyev, First Secretary of the Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the United Nations, during an interactive dialogue with the Chair of the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Special Rapporteur on the rights of persons with disabilities at the Third Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

“Ensuring the full and effective participation of persons with disabilities in society, on an equal basis with others, should be an overarching objective for States and the international community.

Effective measures should be taken in the fields of education, employment, social services, healthcare, public participation, and awareness-raising to ensure the full enjoyment of human rights by persons with disabilities.

This year marks the 20th anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, a landmark treaty that elaborates on the rights of persons with disabilities and sets out a code of implementation.

In Azerbaijan, state policy on disabilities is guided by the principles of inclusivity, integration, equality, non-discrimination, and respect for the characteristics of persons with disabilities.

As a result of reforms undertaken in recent years, negative connotations have been removed from legislative acts, disability governance has been modernised through digital transformation, and Azerbaijani Sign Language has been officially recognised.

While addressing human rights challenges related to disability, it should be noted that the prevalence of newly acquired disabilities is increasing as a result of landmines, explosive remnants of war (ERW), and improvised explosive devices (IEDs), including in post-conflict settings.

More than 13 per cent of Azerbaijan’s territory is contaminated by unexploded ordnance laid during the occupation, posing a serious risk to the returning population. Since 2020, the number of mine victims has reached 443, underscoring the need for international solidarity and support to prevent disability, particularly by strengthening national mine-action efforts.

In conclusion, Azerbaijan will continue to take measures to prevent disabilities, provide habilitation and rehabilitation, and ensure equal opportunities for persons with disabilities,” Shahriyar Hajiyev said in his statement.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 24, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 24. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 28-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev was interviewed by French Figaro newspaper.

- The stockpiles of weapons, ammunition and fuel of Armenian armed forces were destroyed, and Armenian UAVs were neutralized.

- The Armenian armed forces shelled Azerbaijani settlements.

- Video of the destruction of Armenian military equipment during the night was published. An Armenian fighter jet was destroyed.

- Azerbaijan's Gubadly district was shelled using artillery from the territory of Armenia.

- Azerbaijani artillery units continued to inflict crushing blows on the Armenian armed forces.

- Armenian armed forces’ attempt to attack Azerbaijani units was prevented. The Azerbaijani Air Force destroyed Armenian military equipment and infrastructure, as well as combat equipment.

World.title: Azerbaijan chairs Turkic Investment Fund’s Board of Governors (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. The Turkic Investment Fund’s Board of Governors has discussed expanding the Fund’s activities and strengthening investment cooperation among member states at a meeting in Tashkent.

According to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy, Azerbaijan was represented at the meeting by First Deputy Minister of Economy Elnur Aliyev.

The meeting highlighted the Fund’s role in strengthening economic integration across the Turkic world, promoting mutual investment, and implementing joint projects. The participants reviewed efforts to organize the Fund’s operations, expand financing opportunities, and strengthen cooperation with international financial institutions.

Aliyev shared Azerbaijan’s experience in establishing bilateral investment funds with partner countries and proposed strengthening links between these funds and the Turkic Investment Fund, as well as developing joint financing mechanisms. Supporting cross-border projects and small and medium-sized enterprises, financing trade, and promoting lending in national currencies were identified as priority areas. The importance of improving operational efficiency and corporate governance was also emphasized.

The meeting decided to assign the chairmanship of the Board of Governors to Azerbaijan and the vice-chairmanship to Hungary until the end of the next annual meeting.

The Turkic Investment Fund was established under an agreement signed in Ankara in 2023 to expand economic cooperation, mutual investment, and regional trade among member states. Its members are Azerbaijan, Türkiye, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Hungary. The Fund supports small and medium-sized enterprises, infrastructure development, and the financing of joint projects.

World.title: Baku Olive Festival kicks off with three days of food, traditions and concerts (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. The Olive Festival has opened at Baku’s Seaside National Park, bringing together local olive products, live music and an outdoor festive atmosphere. The event runs from October 23 to 25, Trend’s correspondent reports from the venue.

Time to coincide with the start of the olive harvest season, the festival combines gastronomy, culture and entertainment, giving residents and visitors an opportunity to explore Azerbaijan’s olive-growing traditions, discover products from local producers, and enjoy the autumn days with family and friends.

Festival pavilions showcase a variety of olive products from local producers. Visitors can explore the range, learn more about olive cultivation and processing, and sample products that hold a special place in the country’s culinary traditions.

Long associated with abundance and prosperity, olives are the central symbol of the festival. The organizers aim to draw attention to Azerbaijan’s longstanding olive-growing traditions, support local producers and help establish a recognizable national brand in the sector.

The festival, however, offers more than culinary discoveries. Over three days, Baku Boulevard will host musical performances and cultural and entertainment events. Visitors can enjoy live music, works of art and concerts by popular performers, creating a festive atmosphere on the Caspian Sea waterfront.

The music program features well-known Azerbaijani pop singers, performers and bands.

DJ Kamo opened the festivities on October 23, setting an energetic tone for the first day. On October 24, visitors can enjoy performances by Rilay and Mardan Kazimov. The evening program will feature rapper and songwriter Orkhan Zeynalli, Honored Artist Khayyam Nisanov and People's Artist Zulfiyya Khanbabayeva.

The daytime music program on October 25 will feature Wave Band, Teymur Suleymanbeyli and Excellent Band. Azad Shabanov and Zamiq Huseynov will take the stage in the evening, with People's Artist Aygun Kazimova closing the festival.

Each day will offer a distinct musical lineup, ranging from contemporary beats and band performances to popular Azerbaijani pop hits.

The festival is held with the support of the Azerbaijan State Tourism Agency and the Seaside Boulevard Administration, with olive and olive product producers Absheron Olive Gardens and Olivea serving as sponsors.

Hosting the event at Seaside National Park, a popular leisure destination for Baku residents and international tourists, is expected to draw wider attention to local products and national traditions.

The festival runs through October 25, with free admission. Visitors are invited to explore the variety of olive products, enjoy open-air concerts and experience the autumn festivities along Baku Boulevard.

World.title: Suburban echidnas on the prowl as breeding season stretches late
World.content:
People coming across echidnas in suburban Adelaide should not move them in the belief they are helping, a rescue worker says, amid an increase in activity.

Adelaide's echidna population is considered very stable and locally abundant where habitat exists.

But they also roam and use the city's stormwater network to make their way to water and food sources, and while well-meaning people may see them in suburbia and want to move them on, the animals are generally "on a mission" and know where they're going.

"I hate to think how many get moved on because they are species that some people are really scared of," Southern Koala and Echidna Rescue co-founder Mish Simpson said.

"I see online that people have moved one because it was walking down the street, and then you read the comments and someone else moved it, and someone else moved it, and then someone else moved it.

" I'm like, 'This poor thing doesn't want to be in the scrub. Stop taking it to the scrub. It's trying to get somewhere.' "

Ms Simpson said they got a lot of reports of echidnas in people's yards.

"I just say give them half an hour to an hour and there's a good chance it will disappear and people are getting back to me and saying, 'Yep, it's long gone,'" she said.

Mish Simpson is the founder and director of the Southern Koala and Echidna Rescue. (ABC News: Luke Pike)

A Department for Environment and Water spokesperson said the species excelled at navigating and could remember safe routes, "therefore avoiding cars and human traffic".

"They have a wide temporal range of activity in a day and night cycle, so can avoid many urban threats."

She said they were also relatively protected from common urban predators, like cats, dogs and foxes, "by their behavioural and physiological defence adaptations, including curling up and digging in and their sharp spines".

"Because of this, echidnas have maintained their distribution across South Australia when compared with other similar-sized mammals," the spokesperson said.

An echidna with an injured foot under Mish Simpson's care. (Supplied: Southern Koala and Echidna Rescue)

Ms Simpson said in the 10 years she had been rescuing echidnas, she had only seen one case of an injury caused by dogs, in which two had managed to "sadly, bite its beak off".

"Most of the time, the dogs are not determined enough. They get pricked in the face a few times and they give up.

"We used to bring the [attacked echidnas] in because there was blood on the echidna but it always turned out to be the dog's blood."

She said domestic cats, too, were not much of problem because they generally did not know what to do, although feral cats had learnt to "get their paws underneath the echidnas and tear their guts".

Ms Simpson said the most common injuries and rescues she dealt with were echidnas hit by cars, which typically occurred on dark, unlit and windy country roads outside suburbia, "although we did have one killed in a driveway on the weekend, which was really sad".

She said calls from people seeking advice had increased from 76 in 2024, to 212 in 2026, but wondered if it was because people had more awareness of her rescue group.

Breeding later in season

Ms Simpson had also noticed an emerging pattern.

"Their breeding season used to be in winter, but it's September and October that's becoming our busiest time," she said.

In 2025 they cared for 15 echidnas, but last year they had about 40, and only four so far this year.

"Last year it didn't get busy until the springtime so it's definitely interesting," Ms Simpson said.

" We're getting lactating echidnas coming through at the end of the summer and they shouldn't still be having babies at that time, so we're definitely noticing the pattern of how things are changing. "

Studying echidnas' sex lives For 35 years American researcher Peggy Rismiller has been studying Kangaroo Island's echidnas and much of our knowledge about these independent, egg-laying mammals is due to her work.

She recalled how the echidnas they had in care last winter were very inactive.

"They didn't want to eat and they kept going into torpor, which is kind of like their hibernation state," Ms Simpson said.

Torpor allows echidnas to lower their body temperature, heart rate and metabolism to conserve energy and survive months without food.

"So we had to try every trick under the sun to make their enclosures warmer so we could get them eating," Ms Simpson said.

"I wonder if that behaviour is kind of what they're doing in the wild, they're too cold and shutting down and then as it starts to warm up a little bit, that's when they seem to be moving around."

Ms Simpson said echidnas at the moment were "on a mission" and should be left alone — although if one was seen trying to navigate a major arterial route or freeway that might be an exception.

"They're all looking for their mates right now, which again, is really bizarre for it to be happening this late in the season," she said.

The DEW spokesperson said the greatest threats to local echidna populations were vehicle strikes, and habitat loss resulting from "the clearance and degradation of native vegetation associated with development".

"Fallen logs, tree stumps, understorey vegetation and rocky, rubble areas are important habitat features that provide shelter and support ant colonies, a key food source for echidnas," she said.

"Disturbance or landscaping of these areas can reduce habitat quality."

World.title: Breaking: Condition of Helen Haines has improved, hospital says
World.content:
The condition of injured MP Helen Haines has improved from critical to serious but stable after more than four days in hospital.

Ms Haines suffered critical injuries on Monday when she was struck by a vehicle outside her electorate office.

Police allege the incident was a deliberate attack by 43-year-old Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, who faces multiple charges.

On Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Ms Haines's condition had improved and she was now stable.

Ms Haines lost both legs as a result of the crash.

World.title: Nearly 30-year-old Magnum ice cream found in freezer
World.content:
The original Magnum Ego has been a quintessential ice cream in Australian households for decades — a perfect summer's day snack for millions across the country.



The iconic ice cream was introduced in 1998, but was discontinued earlier this year, to the surprise of many.



However, earlier this week, a regional Victorian shop owner struck gold, accidentally stumbling upon an almost 30-year-old Magnum Ego tucked away in the back of his freezer.

Ash Standbridge, the owner of the Kolmar House General Store in Harrow, in Victoria's south-west, discovered the original Magnum Ego from the late '90s.

"At first I was a bit amazed and in a bit of disbelief," he said.

"I was just routinely clearing out a freezer and, as you do, you're chipping away at it and the ice and there was something underneath that I saw and noticed the old logo and the old wrapper and I'm like, 'Well, that's been here a while.'

" And, amazingly, it was still solid and intact; so frozen in time. "

Harrow's Kolmar House is more than 145 years old. (Supplied: Facebook)

Mr Standbridge took over the business just 10 months ago, but the general store has more than 145 years of history.

The ice-cream stick featured vanilla ice cream covered in a thin milk chocolate layer, then a caramel layer and then an outer shell of milk chocolate.

"I was a kid in the late '90s and I remember it being a pretty big deal at the time, it was that sort of top-tier ultimate ice cream that people went crazy for," he said.

"So, as soon as I saw that wrapper, those sorts of memories came flooding back.

"I remember Friday night ice-cream runs to the servo with the family, and we were definitely a Magnum family. I remember the Ego just being that top-tier supreme one."



Mr Standbridge posted the discovery on social media, which went viral, but unlike some courageous individuals in the comments, he said he wasn't brave enough to eat it.



"I ate two a day for a week when they came out," one commented on a Reddit feed.



While another said they "still look for them, and they've been gone for so long", while others recalled walking their "dog 10 times for one Magnum Ego".

Mr Standbridge had contacted the Magnum Ice Cream company about his find, and it is looking into it.

"Australians have been sharing stories, memories and tributes to Magnum Ego, reminding us just how special the product remains to so many people," the company said.

"We've loved seeing the conversation unfold and hearing people's memories of one of Australia's most iconic ice creams.



"For now, all we can say is watch this space."

More historic items found

The finds did not stop with the ice cream. Mr Standbridge managed to uncover multiple souvenirs from over the decades, in the same storeroom the freezer was in.

"I found old chip packets, again from the '80s and '90s," he said.

"I found a flavoured milk that was still sealed, but with no liquid on the inside, so the liquid had disappeared."



Mr Standbridge was in no rush to throw them away, keeping many of the items, which were all part of his store's unique history.

World.title: Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
World.content:
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.

The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.

'You can't be what you can't see' As she prepares for her final Test appearance, Emily Chancellor reflects on the legacy she leaves in Australian women's rugby.

But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.

"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.

"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].

"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.

"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.

"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.

Piper Duck scored one of the Wallaroos' five tries in their 38-31 win over Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.

The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.

But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

World.title: Darwin home owners selling up in nation's 'strongest property market'
World.content:
Lisa-Joy Cron bought her Palmerston home in 2010, just before Darwin's property market crashed — now, with prices rising after more than a decade of stagnation, she's weighing up selling before a possible downturn.

"I think right now is a good time to sell," she said.

"Purely because of the profit I could potentially make, and to take advantage of the good market in the Northern Territory at the moment … particularly with the interest rate rises."

Ms Cron said if she were to sell right now, she hoped her property would go for at least $300,000 more than what she bought it for 16 years ago.

Why housing is the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds.

A growing number of Darwin home owners and investors are listing their properties to cash in on rising prices, but experts at real estate analytics company Cotality warn there may only be a small window to get a good price.

Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said Darwin was defying the national property price slump, recording the "strongest property market in the country".

Property prices increased only modestly for the month of September, with house prices up 0.3 per cent and units up 0.8 per cent.

He said Darwin was now the only capital city where house prices were rising, largely due to limited supply and years of sluggish building activity.

Although more home owners were listing their properties, Mr Burg said there were fewer buyers, indicating the tight property market may be gradually unwinding.

Property prices are continuing to rise in Darwin. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"There is still some uncertainty around where property demand is heading in the coming months," he said.

"There is the risk, of course, that the RBA may do another hike to the interest rates in November, and that would have another further impact.

" So it is possible that Darwin might start to experience the broader national downturn that we're seeing. "

He said the market was already showing signs of cooling.

"At the midpoint of January, [the total number of properties for sale was] around 60 per cent below average," Mr Burg said.

"It's now sitting around 40 per cent below average and is continuing to track up."

Real estate agent Kerri-Ann Laurence, who has sold homes across Darwin for more than two decades, has also noticed an uptick in listings since January but said "historically, it's still quite low".

She said the majority of her clients were either relocating, moving for family reasons, upsizing or downsizing.

Kerri-Ann Laurence has worked in Darwin for more than two decades. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I've no doubts some of the downsizers in particular are seizing the opportunity," she said.

Ms Laurence said she'd also noticed the recent wave of interstate investors — who, over the past year, had been snapping up properties across greater Darwin within days of them being listed — was now easing as prices continued to rise.

However, she said she expected the market to remain on an upward trajectory.

"There's been plenty of projects on the boil — Beetaloo gas is now flowing, I think that will lead to more investment, and in a small town like Darwin, it doesn't take much," she said.

" If one of these projects needs 1,000 [workers] on the ground, that's going to make a dramatic difference in the real estate landscape overnight. "

Darwin remains among the most expensive capital cities to rent a home, ranking third behind Sydney and Perth.

Cost-of-living pressure 'entrenching disadvantage' in the NT The NT has some of the country's most expensive rental costs, with households having to set aside more of their weekly wages to cover the price of essentials.

Cotality's latest data revealed the median dwelling rental cost rose by about 11.6 per cent year on year, as of September.

The Top End city's vacancy rate remained tight, sitting at about 1.9 per cent, Mr Burg said.

"That means that in some locations in Darwin, it is actually cheaper to purchase the house under a mortgage than it is to rent a similar property," he said.

The shortfall in new home construction paints a bleaker picture for renters outside the capital, with the vacancy rate in Alice Springs sitting at just 1.4 per cent.

World.title: Vintage car rally celebrates the Ford Model A
World.content:
Dozens of vintage cars have descended on Western Australia's far south coast in the country's largest gathering of Ford Model As.

It was a rare glimpse into the past for the early colonial town of Albany, 400 kilometres south of Perth, with the sounds of vintage car horns flooding its historic precinct on Friday.

Model As line up in Albany for the vintage car rally. (ABC News: Rachel Jennings)

Rally director Andrae Moore said some of the restored cars travelled from nearly every state in the country, while others came from further away.

"Then we've had participants actually join us without their cars from New Zealand, the United Kingdom and Slovenia," she said.

Andrae Moore says dozens of cars took part in the rally. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Century of preservation

Produced in the early 1900s, the Model A was one of the most well-known and top-selling cars in America.

"All the [second] Model As are from 1928 through to 1931 and came after the infamous Model T," Ms Moore said.

Ford Model A enthusiasts from across the globe travelled to Albany for the rally. (ABC News: Rachel Jennings)

" These cars were special because they were the everyman's car, and they were allowed to be in any colour — they didn't have to be black like the Model T. "

For many of the members, the cars are treasured possessions and owned to be driven.

Eighty-two-year-old Ben Munneke estimated he drove his Model A 5,000 kilometres from Maleny in Queensland to Albany for the rally.

"It was good fun driving, a lot of stops along the Nullarbor; there's not a lot of comfortable places to stay, but we made it, and we enjoyed doing it," he said.

Flags of origin on display

For Steve Watson and his friends, the travel was much further as they flew from Yorkshire in England and borrowed a car so they could take part in the event.

"We have borrowed a car, and we've adorned it with suitable patriotic flags so everybody knows where we've come from," he said.

Steve Watson travelled all the way from Yorkshire in the UK to join the rally. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Watson said there were similar clubs in the UK but not at the same level as the Australian meeting.

"There is a Model A club in England, and we have about 300 members, but the participation in an event like this is not as good," he said.

World.title: Barra Bonanza organisers eager for channel works after 15 years of silt
World.content:
Hundreds of anglers have hit the water at Cardwell this weekend for the 20th annual Barra Bonanza.

The two-day catch-and-release fishing event drew record numbers this year, with more than 350 participants on the water and the most female entrants in the competition's history.

Most of the boats launched from Port Hinchinbrook before 6am on Friday. After that, the channel could become inaccessible.

The Port Hinchinbrook marina has been in disarray since Cyclone Yasi crossed the coast in 2011.

The channel has been choked by mud and silt, limiting access for boats wanting to get in and out.

As the boat access is tidal, competitors must keep one eye on the fishing and the other on the tide. If they miss the high-tide window, they could find themselves stuck on the water's edge.

Vessels are unable to get in and out of the water for most of the day from Port Hinchinbrook. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Cardwell Sportfishing Club president Greb Abbs said organisers had to consider this when planning the event.

He said they checked the tides a year out to determine the best date for the event.

"There's two things that we look for: the best time to go fishing, which is around the moon, and how it coincides with the tide," he said.

"We set the tournament up so that it's for the fishermen to have the best opportunity to catch fish and for the best opportunity to get in and out."

Port Hinchinbrook's recovery and redevelopment have been riddled with political and legal complications.

The Port Hinchinbrook boat ramp was a hive of activity. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

The state government recently acquired the land and allocated $64 million in the budget to restore the port, including dredging its waterways.

Early works have been completed, and tenders for a dredging contractor closed in September.

Fishing club vice-president Jeff Snell said if the project went ahead, it would be a game changer for the town.

"[It is] the best thing that could happen around here," he said.

"The whole place was just bloody pumping before [Cyclone Yasi] and now it's going to bring that back again."

Jeff Snell believes dredging the port would boost the coastal town's economy. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

Mr Abbs said the ability to have access to the port in all tides would also make it safer because the coast guard would be able to get on the water if there was an incident, instead of having to rely on nearby crews in Tully and Innisfail to step in when the tide was too low.

Environmental concerns

Environmentalists have warned dredging the port could cause serious harm to waterways and the animals living in the channel.

Retired engineer and local environmentalist, John Mewing, said he thought the government had been secretive.

"The difficulty that I had in getting hold of the information that I now have appears to me that the government wanted to keep a lot of these submissions secret," he said.

John Mewing fears dredging the port will adversely impact the region's waterways and marine life. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

He said he had been seeking information about a full environmental impact assessment, both on and off site, and what ramifications there would be if the project proceeded.

Mr Mewing, a keen fisherman himself, said there was no need to disrupt nature to allow easier access to the channel.

"Right beside this development, we've got a listed World Heritage Area in the Hinchinbrook Channel," he said.

"It should be obvious to anyone who visits this area that this is a relatively pristine wilderness.

"That in itself should be enough to say to everyone that this is not a place for a development like this to happen."

Member for Hinchinbrook Wayde Cheisa was contacted for comment.

20 years of community

The Cardwell Barra Bonanza was founded by ex-club president Chris Stoter and local business owner Mick Volp, with the aim of boosting tourism in the region.

Mr Stoter said it had been amazing to watch the event grow.

"I'm pretty chuffed. I get emotional when you walk in there and you see all [the] people," he said.

"I never thought in 20 years' time I'd be sitting here doing this. We just took it under our wing and ran with it."

The pair came up with the idea over a Boxing Day beer.

Mick Volp and Chris Stoter started the tournament 20 years ago. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

"I think when we first kicked it off, Chris said to me, 'This is what I want to do,'" Mr Volp said.

"I said, 'Well, you organise the fishing side of it, I'll organise the sponsorship side.'

"We're just glad to be able to put something back into Cardwell."

Both agreed it would be wonderful to see Port Hinchinbrook restored as they reflected on the glory days before Cyclone Yasi.

"People would line up down the marina, there'd be hundreds of people … the restaurant was nearly at full capacity all week," Mr Stoter said.

"That was all due to the easy [channel] access as well, and the Hinchinbrook [Island], really … it's some pretty spectacular viewing."

He said he was "stoked" at the prospect of the port being dredged and seeing the town come alive again.

World.title: Man with 10,000 succulents shares secrets to keeping them happy
World.content:
A pop of colour from an indoor plant is a staple in many households.

From apartments to smaller backyards, the way Australians are living has resulted in a surge in succulent popularity over the past decade.

For newly retired Ian Andrews, who lives in Renmark in South Australia's Riverland, his five-year gardening plan to propagate the plant has quickly become an obsession.

Now the owner of more than 10,000 succulents, he said the benefits of the resilient and striking species were endless.

Ian Andrews is a big believer that plants live naturally outside so that is where they should stay. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"Australia has a very diverse climate, but we tend to have cold and wet winters and drier summers which are favourable to many succulent families," he said.

"In the Riverland for example, a lot of succulents come from the southern part of Africa, so their soils and climates are very similar."

Not only has the hobby reinvigorated his passion for plants, but it has helped him transition into retirement.

"Retirement's been lovely. [My garden] is my Zen area," he said.

Ian Andrews has always had a passion for plants but was not able to indulge it fully until retirement. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Waltes)

"[I've gone] from being self-employed when we started our business 25 years ago, which was often seven days a week … to being able to catch up and start doing things that most people take for granted.

"It's a positive thing rather than sitting on the internet gambling the money away or down all those other bad habits that you can develop."

Many who have visited Mr Andrews's colourful display want to know his secret to succulent success.

"Give them lots of outdoor breaks. If you have them inside for a week, take it outside for a month," he said.

Ian Andrews says leaving succulents alone can often be the best form of care. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"Succulents are easier to look after and are more forgiving.

" Sometimes they can look better when you come home from a holiday because they've had time to dry out. "

Growing in popularity

Greenlife Industry NSW & ACT chief executive Mike Mehigan said plant sales in Australia were worth more than $3 billion.

He said the commercial sector and nursery sector were performing well, with younger generations driving demand.

Mike Mehigan says succulents are a great way to start learning about plants. (Supplied: Mike Mehigan)

"The number of plants being sold has probably never been greater than it is at the moment," he said.

Succulent demand has been on the rise for the past 10 years, with housing changes likely a factor.

"The way we live nowadays, people often don't have gardens, and there are a lot more people living in apartments where balconies or indoors is often where they have to grow their plants," Mr Mehigan said.

Hybrid Aeoniums are Ian Andrews's favourite. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"I think young people [also tend to] have plants in their bedrooms, and small succulents are a great way to start."

The way in which people are purchasing their plants is evolving in Australia, with many opting for online purchases.

"To sit on your couch in the evening and order your plants is just the way we do things nowadays, and although [plants are] quite a traditional sort of product, we're selling them in a modern way," Mr Mehigan said.

Back in Renmark, Mr Andrews said it was never too late to get a green thumb.

"Gardening is always there for you when you have got time and if something takes your fancy, give it a go," he said.

"At the end of the day, a plant might die, but you can just go and buy another one."

WorldEuropePrince William Prince William reveals he once dreamt of being ‘DJ Xara’ or a career as a policeman David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: Prince William has revealed he once dreamt of becoming a policeman or a DJ when he considered careers other than being heir to the throne. The Prince of Wales said he came up with a disc jockey stage name, “DJ Xara”, but never managed to play a big event. Prince William (left) made a surprise appearance alongside Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on Graham Norton’s TV chat show. Instagram Asked by television host Graham Norton if he ever DJ’ed at school parties, William replied: “No, I didn’t, I never got that good.” The talk about the prince’s early aspirations came up when he joined guests Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on Norton’s weekly BBC television show on Friday night (early on Saturday, AEDT).



Waddingham, one of the stars of the Ted Lasso television series, told the prince his “DJ Xara” name was “rubbish” – to which he did not disagree. Irwin, the son of crocodile hunter Steve Irwin and a winner of the British version of Dancing with the Stars, suggested the prince might have dreamt about wrangling crocodiles. Loading “If I’d met you earlier, I might have,” the prince replied. The appearance was a rare move for William to join a late-night talk show that usually features stage and screen stars speaking about their latest productions.



The prince, born in 1982, discussed his DJ career ideas when Norton asked whether he had ever wondered about doing a job other than the one he was assigned at birth. “Being a policeman, I thought, was quite cool,” the prince replied. “And then I went through a phase when I wanted to be a DJ, which didn’t go very well.” Blanchett, who has gained rave reviews for her appearance in Elektra/Person at the National Theatre in London, joked with William about whether he had stage moves to go with his “DJ Xara” name. The prince joined the talk show to promote the Earthshot Prize, a climate project he set up in 2020 and which is backed by Blanchett, Waddingham and Irwin.



Related Article Royal family Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’ The organisation raises funds from sponsors and selects 15 finalists each year with environmental projects around the world. It then chooses five winners and gives each one a £1 million ($1.9 million) grant. Two Australian projects have made the longlist in recent years: the Indigenous Desert Alliance and the Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney. William has also announced an Earthshot Prize for children, ahead of the annual Earthshot Prize announcements at a ceremony in Mumbai, India on November 17. “For many years I was hearing stories about environment issues and one thing that struck me was the negativity and doom, which got me down,” he told Norton. “I thought we could do something more powerful and more optimistic, and the idea of an awards ceremony came about, and we could talk about urgency and optimism together. It’s all about getting excited.



“There are some amazing people out there doing things to protect the world. We could really highlight what is being done and scale them to the next level to have more impact around the world.” I’m your fan: William revealed a love of director Christopher Nolan (right) and his Dark Knight series. The prince also discussed pop culture and film, including the films of director Christopher Nolan, when asked how he “switched off” from royal life. “It is music and film. I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films,” he said. “I like action films too, but I like something a bit different. I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – The Dark Knight series is psychologically dark and deep, and I absolutely love that.



“He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Bad taste as Powerhouse cookery book misses deadline
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWArts Bad taste as Powerhouse cookery book misses deadline Clair Weaver October 24, 2026 — 9:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. When Julie Gibbs was running Penguin’s lifestyle imprint Lantern, she declared cookbooks could take “anything from 18 months to four years” to complete. It was an estimate borne of experience: the cookbook guru had published big culinary names including Kylie Kwong, Matt Moran, Maggie Beer and Stephanie Alexander. “It is important to choose ideas with staying power,” she said. Today her comments, from an interview with digital publication The Design Files in 2013, have come back to bite her. Former cookbook publisher Julie Gibbs, who has been working on the Australian Culinary Archive for seven years. juliegibbs.com For the past seven years, Gibbs has been working on the Australian Culinary Archive: a $1.5 million dollar project supported by taxpayer funding that was supposed to culminate in a “landmark” book to coincide with the Powerhouse Parramatta’s much-anticipated opening on November 7. But the Herald can reveal there is no sign of the book, which has been in the works for four of those years. “The Powerhouse looks forward to launching the publication in 2027,” a spokesperson said.



Yet last year, the museum still hoped to meet the publication deadline. “To coincide with the launch of Powerhouse Parramatta, Powerhouse Publishing will release a landmark publication – The Australian Culinary Archive (working title),” it said in a description of the role of archive advisor published in March last year, which was awarded to Gibbs. In two separate roles published in October last year, the Powerhouse sought an editorial advisor and editorial support and proofreading services for “a 1000-page publication that documents the Australian Culinary Archive”. The project was described as “nearing completion”. (Left to right) Julie Gibbs, Kate Gibbs (food author and granddaughter of Margaret Fulton), Guy Grossi, Lisa Havilah, Neil Perry, Louise Keats, Suzanne Gibbs, Peter Gilmore and Kylie Kwong gathered to mark the launch of the Australian Culinary Archive in 2020. Louie Douvis According to the Powerhouse’s website, France-based Australian food writer Libby Travers has been collaborating with Gibbs on the book “over the past few years”. Travers wrote on her personal blog about a 2024 research trip to the elBulli museum in Spain.



“I was there to look at the ways in which culinary history and culture can be recorded and represented – a research trip for the book I am writing with the erudite and exceptional Julie Gibbs,” she wrote. “It is a book that will tell the story of the past 50 years of cooking in Australia via the Powerhouse Museum’s Culinary Archive.” A Powerhouse spokesperson confirmed Gibbs has been involved with developing the archive and book since 2019, while Travers was engaged to edit the book and then as editorial advisor but was not paid travel or research fees. “The archive has been under development for seven years ... at an average annual cost of $120k per year including acquisitions, fees, and domestic travel,” the spokesperson said. “A publication to present this archive is currently in development. This has been a four-year project. The total cost is about $165k per year including editorial, design, photography, typesetting, rights and clearances costs. The rights, clearances and permissions process has been complex as it relates to materials for items that are up to 50 years old and is ongoing.” These figures - totalling $840,000 for the archive and $660,000 for the book - do not include internal museum costs, such as staffing.



Related Article Exclusive

Arts Powerhouse slammed over Kylie Kwong’s new $440,000 ambassador role Questions over the book come amid heightened scrutiny on the museum over budget concerns. On October 13, the Herald revealed Kwong had been awarded a $440,000 contract to be a culinary ambassador for the Powerhouse a month after then CEO Lisa Havilah said her involvement was due to end. Kwong has previously had cookbooks published by Gibbs, who described the chef as “my bestie” on social media in 2014. The Herald does not suggest either of the women participated in wrongdoing. Havilah has stepped aside from her role pending “investigations into governance and procurement”, with NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin stepping in as acting CEO and NSW Treasury executive Cassandra Wilkinson parachuted in as chief operating officer. In 2020, it was estimated the archive would take “at least two years to collect” before items would be catalogued and digitised at the museum.



Whisk used by Damien Pignolet from the Australian Culinary Archive Powerhouse Designed to be “a living record of the people who have shaped Australia’s food culture”, it includes material from chefs, producers, vendors, writers, photographers, critics and diners. Objects collected include a whisk from Gibbs’ chef ex-husband Damian Pignolet, a label for chocolates sold by Sean Moran and a stool from Kwong’s restaurant Billy Kwong. Gibbs has had three contracts in her tenure at the Powerhouse. First she was head consultant for the archive, then an “artistic associate” as part of a controversial $2.6 million program that was terminated, and since last year archive advisor. Her current contract expires in July next year, with an option to extend it by another year. When she was awarded her first role, Gibbs told the Herald’s Good Food she felt “like the luckiest person in the world”, adding “I’m travelling all over Australia to interview incredibly influential people about the paths they’ve trodden and see what treasures are hiding in their storerooms and cupboards”. World.title: I try not to complain about crime in London – an ancestor of mine snatched and ran
World.content:
WorldEuropeLondon I try not to complain about crime in London – an ancestor of mine snatched and ran David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. London: The conditions look perfect when I walk up from the underground to search for London crime. The sun is out, and so are the crowds. The footpaths around the Bond Street tube station are jammed with shoppers heading to the big department stores nearby, while tourists linger at the souvenir stores. I can see why this neighbourhood is known for mobile phone theft. Some pedestrians are glancing at their screens as they walk, and some stop to take selfies along Oxford Street, holding their phones out near the kerb. That seems risky in a city with almost 200 cases of phone theft and robbery each day. Stan Blake, a former building worker who sells The Big Issue magazine along London’s Marylebone Lane, says he sees theft on most days. David Crowe But I’m searching for the scene of an older crime. I find it when I get to the corner of Oxford Street and Gee’s Court, a tiny passageway leading to a pedestrian mall. Here, two centuries ago, an ancestor of mine took up a common trade on these streets. He snatched and ran.



William Daley, 17, was a young Irish lad at work with an even younger accomplice. Together, they found a target on Oxford Street in the winter of 1818. England was at peace after defeating Napoleon, but London was ravaged by crushing poverty – and a small square of silk could be worth about two days’ wages. The target, George Reid, did not even notice the younger thief steal his handkerchief. But a worker nearby saw exactly what happened: the boy took the silk and passed it quickly to Daley, who slipped it into his hat and walked on in the hope of a swift getaway along Oxford Street. That walk turned into a run, however, when Reid called for help. “Stop, thief!” he yelled. A transcript from the trial of William Daley on theft charges at the Old Bailey in 1818, including the eyewitness accounts of the crime. He was sentenced to transportation to Australia for life. David Crowe Daley ran from Oxford Street towards Marylebone Lane, a curved street of stores and pubs. A policeman then made an arrest that changed history – at least in my family. “I heard the alarm, and saw the prisoner running up Marylebone Lane,” the constable told a court a few weeks later. “He was stopped, and the handkerchief fell out of his hat.” We know this because the Old Bailey, in a testament to British justice, kept the transcript from Daley’s appearance in court. The sentence for stealing a silk handkerchief with a value of seven shillings? “Transported for life.” Daley was on a ship to the colonies in July, and he arrived in Sydney on New Year’s Eve. He may not have felt like celebrating.



It seems like a story from Charles Dickens, although Oliver Twist did not appear until 20 years later. In that tale, the hero is found to be of high birth and inherits a fortune, but there was no secret family wealth for Daley. He was sent to work on the farms west of Sydney as a convict labourer before eventually gaining his ticket of leave. At least things did not end badly: he married, became a farmer and died at 70 near Windsor. Related Article Crime Is London finally winning its mobile phone theft war? I think about that life-changing punishment as I walk down Marylebone Lane. Some of the shop workers around here tell me they rarely see a thief being caught. One of the bar staff at the Spread Eagle, a nearby pub, says she sees a phone being stolen on most nights when she finishes her shift. A thief will speed past on an electric scooter or bike, snatch a phone and race away. The Metropolitan Police release videos showing brazen thefts in busy areas like Oxford Street, but they say they are cracking down. “Phone theft and robbery fell from 81,439 offences in 2024 to 71,867 in 2025,” they say. It looks like falling again this year, judging by the tally to August. This seems to add to the progress we reported last year. In one celebrated case, the victim of a phone theft helped guide police to a warehouse at Heathrow Airport using a “find my phone” feature. Remarkably, the phone was left on, and the location signal was still working, so police were able to arrest a gang responsible for shipping around 40,000 phones to China. The three men were sentenced last month to prison terms of up to nine years.



While the official numbers say things are getting better, it is hard to be sure. So I talk to someone who sees a lot of what happens on these streets. Stan Blake, 61, has been selling The Big Issue near Marylebone Lane for about three years. Raised in Wales, he was a builder but lost his job and now relies on magazine sales for his living. Related Article Opinion

Charity I was too busy for the charity vendor. But he said something that stopped me in my tracks Stephen Brook Special correspondent, The Age Just last week, he saw two police cars chasing a man on a scooter who had allegedly just stolen five phones. A few years ago, he watched in disbelief as a thief snatched the phone of a woman trying to pay for The Big Issue using Blake’s mobile payment device. He lent her his phone so she could call for help. Has he ever seen anyone chase a thief and recover a phone? “No, they’ve always got away,” he says. This is a key reason why mobile phone theft is such a talking point in London: many people are worried authorities are not bringing people to justice; that there is a breakdown in law and order. In a sense, the silk handkerchief was the mobile phone of its day: a small and relatively common item of high value. The difference is that today’s bikes and scooters seem to guarantee a quick escape. And with so many tourists in this city, the thieves are never short of targets.



I cannot say I like it, but I try not to complain about crime in London. Where would I be without it? Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
