World.title: In her new book, Pachinko author Min Jin Lee takes on the tyranny of ambition
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature In her new book, Pachinko author Min Jin Lee takes on the tyranny of ambition Declan Fry October 24, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Speaking from her home in Harlem, New York, Min Jin Lee asks if it’s a good time to call. It’s a perfect time. Commiserating about time differences, I recall visiting a (very cold) Harlem years ago, where I accidentally mistook someone’s wash detergent for communal use. Min’s voice picks up at this juicy gossip. She has no New Yorker-berating to share (the woman at the laundromat really chewed me out) but she admits – despite everyone telling her it has an “attitude” – feeling that Melbourne is nice. Author Min Jin Lee. Hae Ran of Channel Yes “I love Australia. People are so open. You can get into a fight with someone in a train here by looking at them wrong. Everyone told me Melbourne is like the New York of Australia because they’re very artistic and intellectual and cool. They meant cool as in avant-garde – but they also meant it as in, a little more chilly,” she says, laughing.“People aren’t triggered at a laundromat by using 10 cents worth of soap. Then again, I do sort of assume in life that everyone is cooler than me.” Her contentment with not being the coolest person in the room speaks to the generosity that drives her. In her 2007 debut, Free Food for Millionaires, and 2017’s bestselling Pachinko, the fortunes of people striving to change their lives in a tumultuous world are the focus. At the heart of her new novel, American Hagwon, are the Kohs, a well-off family brought down in the world after the Asian financial crisis. As they move from Seoul to Sydney and then California through the 1990s and the early years of this century, their relationships are subject to the tyranny of distance. Boarding schools offer the opportunity for a new life but also distance from the family home. White-collar workers are liable to suddenly wind up working in fast food joints. Wherever the Koh children live – studious Bo, athletic DH, artistically minded Mido – education is not just a matter of aspiration but a continual struggle of re-evaluation and self-reflection. The hagwon, a Korean cram school, becomes symbolic of the promise of another life. Australia, Lee says, offered a fascinating social experiment in which to set much of the novel – especially as an alternative to the more ruthless aspects of American society. Among her affections in this regard she counts HECS, TAFE (“genius” for offering vocational rights sans university – “I was so, so impressed”) and mandatory voting (“the sausage sizzle!”).



“There’s a reason why even the coolest person in Melbourne is probably warmer and more relaxed than a New Yorker – [in the US] you have to bankrupt yourself to get your cancer treated. If I give a speech about violence against Asian-Americans, or lobby for reproductive rights, which is under threat in America, I pay the price of that as a writer,” she says. “It’s really difficult to survive. In America, if your employer doesn’t give you the time to vote, you can’t vote. To me, it’s not a true democracy.” She’s not unaware of the White Australia policy or Indigenous dispossession, she says. But truths coexist. Animating Min’s writing is her tangible sense of compassion. You don’t know what people are going through, she says. Someone may look fine but have troubles that are not visible on the surface. “I want to persuade people to recognise the full humanity of people who have been very invisible. I also wanted to show the lie behind it. You can have this highly selective education and yet end up working as a fried fish cook. You get old. No one wants you. I’m talking about being made obsolete in the era of capitalism.” Lee bemoans the loss of play and of third spaces, of less rabidly competitive and structured lives. It is possible – indeed almost normal now – to walk through streets where people wander alone, haloed by phone light, returning to homes whose other occupants have long since retreated to their own isolation. The world is becoming automated and predetermined in a way where even the attempt to escape isolation – to ask for a human being at a shop, to seek almost any form of human contact, physical or otherwise – is treated as a perverse eccentricity rather than an essential element of life.



“People need to play. It’s really sad when I hear someone ask, ‘how did you get your job? What did you do?’ As if they could reverse engineer the process. I look at them and I kind of think, ‘it doesn’t really work that way’. People are fairly circuitous. And the people who are good at what they do are often more circuitous,” she says with a laugh. “I’ve seen so many people with selective education break down. They tend to be the most direct, process-wise. You think they’ll go far in life. And it just does not work out. ” I mention that a character like Mido – who has no intention of entering the theatre but finds, when she begins writing scenes in Sydney, that she is forced to think about everyone else in the scene and even the people offstage – connects to one of the book’s epigraphs: a 1963 James Baldwin lecture about how, as one is educated, one begins examining the society in which one lives. Min Jin Lee in New York last month. Getty Images for Spotify “Yes! Oh my gosh, that scene was such a hard one to write. My novels are Trojan horses. I really am trying so hard to say, ‘please look at this’. Please look at how we are destroying ourselves. It’s a radical gesture just to live the life you didn’t think you could live. We lose so much when we have cynical young people who have been heartbroken by what our generation has delivered to them. I really do think it’s possible to fix this. But it’s going to take us older people reaching out to them. We have to take care of children who are not our children.” The seduction of believing that education – a nice job, a certain decision – can protect or shelter you is precarious, Lee says. Especially in neoliberal environments where, in the absence of regulation, the conditions of life and existence itself “can become a kind of hell”.



“The only people I really saw survive the IMF crisis who didn’t have generational wealth – which destroyed so many paths – are those who would choose a different path.” Lee interviewed many people in writing the book, she says. She met people like John, the family patriarch, cornered by economic crises out of their control. Many of those who fell came from the middle class, people who had been taught to believe in the promises of the social compact. “Literature all the time is saying: look at the character. Look at the context. I want to know what people are doing when no one’s looking. And also look at the fact there are so many contradictions.” Related Article Review Need a new book? Our picks of the latest fiction and non-fiction books Yet research has limits, and the imagination has to go where research cannot. In size and scope, American Hagwon is comparable to the big, baggy monsters of 19th-century realism. Balzac’s Human Comedy. Zola. Like the celebrated novels of that era, it is also a story of class and upward mobility. Unlike them, though, it is written in a plainspoken style. Lee describes the precision of its sentences – what she calls “clean” writing – as acting in service to the delivery of the message. She looks to the nonfiction of Joan Didion and V.S. Naipaul, she says, to find ways of delivering the same immersive qualities of authors like Zola and Hardy without their grand, omniscient narrative style. “I want it to be so clean that there’s actually no room for misinterpretation. I’d like it if you don’t even think about me. To just be about the story.” Before she has to go, we talk about some of our shared loves. “I like dogs,” she says. “I like children. I think adults are kind of scary sometimes, but mostly they mean well. That’s the way I look at things.”



Truer words have never been spoken. American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee (4th Estate, $38) is available now. What else is happening in the book world? World.title: Deadly shooting outside Paris a ‘terrorist attack’, say police
World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime Deadly shooting outside Paris a ‘terrorist attack’, say police David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 6:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: A gunman has killed one victim and wounded five others in an outer suburb of Paris known for its migrant communities, prompting public warnings of a terror attack in the wake of violent protests. Police arrested the alleged killer after a frenzy of drive-by shootings that left one 12-year-old girl fighting for her life. Forensic investigators search for evidence after a shooting in Trappes, outside Paris. AP French President Emmanuel Macron described the shootings as a “racist terrorist attack” in the areas of Trappes and Yvelines, south-west of the Paris city centre, and warned of the pressure on the nation from weeks of unrest. Police said they were treating the attack as terrorism and were aware of reports that the killer had set traps in his home to kill visitors that he expected to investigate him after the shootings. Police also detained one of his family members.



The shootings on Friday (French time) came on the eve of another series of protests and rallies due to be held on Saturday in Paris and other cities over the cost of living and school funding. Worried about another outbreak of violence and looting, the French government has mobilised 70,000 police to guard against rioting, while authorities in Lyon and Marseilles have banned the marches. French President Emmanuel Macron meets community members at the town hall in Trappes after the shooting. Reuters Authorities did not draw a direct link between the riots and the shootings, but the attack in the Paris suburbs came after a week of debate about whether migrants were among the looters who smashed stores last weekend. Macron spoke of a “turning point in our republic and our nation” as a result of the terror attack.



Mayor Nicolas Dainville, whose local government of La Verriere includes Yvelines, said the attack was another sign of the pressure on French unity after the protests. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated “A racist motive seems clear, given that here in La Verriere three individuals of African descent were targeted,” he told Franceinfo. “This points to a very serious situation in France, a country that is fractured and divided. “The atmosphere we are currently living in – in which the mayors, in their own modest way, are trying to address – is truly critical.”



National police union spokesman Rudy Manna told Franceinfo the gunman fired multiple times at people walking on the street who had done nothing to provoke him. Manna said the evidence suggested the gunman also intended to kill a police officer. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned on Friday about the risk of further violence in protests on Saturday, accusing ultra-left groups of encouraging violence and looting. More than 3000 stores were damaged or looted last weekend after protests turned violent across the country. Police arrested 2700 people, about 70 per cent of them adults.



Related Article Analysis

Paris protests The violence of the streets of Paris looked like rage. It revealed a society that will take years to heal “We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence,” Nunez told reporters on Friday after meetings with Macron and other government leaders. Nunez said authorities had identified online calls from hard-left groups that encouraged activists to target public buildings. “We are not ​talking about a nice, friendly demonstration,” he said. “We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and ⁠we will let absolutely nothing pass.”



Police have authorised ​a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday but have insisted it take place away from the Place de la Republique, an area that was a focal point of the riots last weekend and has been under curfew since then. Authorities rejected requests for rallies in Paris by the main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018. Many French cities beyond Paris have also banned protests, including France’s second- and third-largest cities, Marseille and Lyon. Nunez ‌said 10,000 more ⁠police would be on the streets than a week ago. With Reuters

World.title: Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk
World.content:
Perspective PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk Matt Dennien October 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Approaching the halfway milestone of Queensland’s four-year electoral cycle, Premier David Crisafulli has spent the past week doing plenty of talking – in speech after set-piece speech. He has spent it talking about what his government has done, and what it’s yet to do. The latter involves fixing the more nebulous “crises” he rode to power vowing to address. “The big four issues that I spoke about before the election remain the big four issues and the big four challenges,” Crisafulli said at his 2026 CEDA State of the State address on Monday. Over a week of speeches, Premier David Crisafulli stayed resolutely on message. AAPIMAGE “And on all of them [health, housing, crime and cost of living], we are making progress after a long period of time where the numbers went in the wrong direction.”



While Crisafulli can cite numbers heading in a better direction – and did, across several other major speeches this week, including to the property and local government sectors – more than anyone else, he should know the limits of relying on statistics. During a Queensland Media Club appearance on Wednesday billed as featuring a “significant policy announcement” in the law and order space, no such thing came, beyond confirmation the parliament will pass a government bill next week. Nor was there anything new in any other area. ‘I want to talk today about what I call a trio of opportunities: fuel, critical minerals, and data centres. All three have challenges. All three have opportunities.’ Crisafulli in his Monday State of the State speech This is the bind in which the government now finds itself: a list of concrete election platform items already all-but ticked off, leaving them either pushing ahead with new policy efforts in areas plaguing governments across the country and globe, or hoping its “let us cook” line finds sympathy. s are still running for the work of the “new Queensland government”, but frustrations over this positioning are beginning to emerge – particularly on crime, where the LNP set the terms of the debate while in opposition, yet admits that public dissatisfaction remains, two years on.





Crisafulli and his strategists seem to believe these glimpses beyond the pre-election picture they painted are too minor to spook a wider population wary of action that’s too swift or extreme. The Labor opposition, led for now by Steven Miles, seems stuck on a small-target strategy, hoping that something – or an accumulation of things – will suddenly become too much for people to bear. The resignation from cabinet of Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm may be the first bit of bark taken from Crisafulli that Labor would view as a win. While Crisafulli’s LNP remain the clear favourites in this masthead’s regular Resolve Political Monitor, that polling also shows the broader mood has soured across a year that has thrown no shortage of extra problems at households and governments.



After significant improvement following the 2024 vote, the outlook for the next year or so among those surveyed for both their personal lives, and the state more broadly, has since returned to pre-election levels. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership Almost more people think things will get worse in their lives than not change, and both cohorts are double the size of those who think it will get better. Compared to before the election, their view of the state’s future is now more pessimistic. The tectonic plates long holding the two-party system in place appear their shakiest since Queensland saw Pauline Hanson’s best yet showing in an Australian parliament three decades ago. So two years could be a long time – for all involved. How do you act, or give the appearance of acting, on fundamental social and economic problems in a way that makes people feel things have changed for the better, when you are also cautious of moving too fast or too far, let alone actually change things for the long-term good?



The Crisafulli government may have a swathe of state and national elections across the country to learn from before it has to face voters for the first time from office, but a bet on people’s willingness to wait to feel change while being told it is happening is no longer such a sure thing. World.title: Prince William reveals he once dreamt of being ‘DJ Xara’ or a career as a policeman
World.content:
WorldEuropePrince William Prince William reveals he once dreamt of being ‘DJ Xara’ or a career as a policeman David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: Prince William has revealed he once dreamt of becoming a policeman or a DJ when he considered careers other than being heir to the throne. The Prince of Wales said he came up with a disc jockey stage name, “DJ Xara”, but never managed to play a big event. Prince William (left) made a surprise appearance alongside Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on Graham Norton’s TV chat show. Instagram Asked by television host Graham Norton if he ever DJ’ed at school parties, William replied: “No, I didn’t, I never got that good.” The talk about the prince’s early aspirations came up when he joined guests Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on Norton’s weekly BBC television show on Friday night (early on Saturday, AEDT).



Waddingham, one of the stars of the Ted Lasso television series, told the prince his “DJ Xara” name was “rubbish” – to which he did not disagree. Irwin, the son of crocodile hunter Steve Irwin and a winner of the British version of Dancing with the Stars, suggested the prince might have dreamt about wrangling crocodiles. Loading “If I’d met you earlier, I might have,” the prince replied. The appearance was a rare move for William to join a late-night talk show that usually features stage and screen stars speaking about their latest productions.



The prince, born in 1982, discussed his DJ career ideas when Norton asked whether he had ever wondered about doing a job other than the one he was assigned at birth. “Being a policeman, I thought, was quite cool,” the prince replied. “And then I went through a phase when I wanted to be a DJ, which didn’t go very well.” Blanchett, who has gained rave reviews for her appearance in Elektra/Person at the National Theatre in London, joked with William about whether he had stage moves to go with his “DJ Xara” name. The prince joined the talk show to promote the Earthshot Prize, a climate project he set up in 2020 and which is backed by Blanchett, Waddingham and Irwin.



Related Article Royal family Prince Harry: ‘I want family reconciliation ... but some people don’t’ The organisation raises funds from sponsors and selects 15 finalists each year with environmental projects around the world. It then chooses five winners and gives each one a £1 million ($1.9 million) grant. Two Australian projects have made the longlist in recent years: the Indigenous Desert Alliance and the Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney. William has also announced an Earthshot Prize for children, ahead of the annual Earthshot Prize announcements at a ceremony in Mumbai, India on November 17. “For many years I was hearing stories about environment issues and one thing that struck me was the negativity and doom, which got me down,” he told Norton. “I thought we could do something more powerful and more optimistic, and the idea of an awards ceremony came about, and we could talk about urgency and optimism together. It’s all about getting excited.



“There are some amazing people out there doing things to protect the world. We could really highlight what is being done and scale them to the next level to have more impact around the world.” I’m your fan: William revealed a love of director Christopher Nolan (right) and his Dark Knight series. The prince also discussed pop culture and film, including the films of director Christopher Nolan, when asked how he “switched off” from royal life. “It is music and film. I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films,” he said. “I like action films too, but I like something a bit different. I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – The Dark Knight series is psychologically dark and deep, and I absolutely love that.



“He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Bad taste as Powerhouse cookery book misses deadline
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWArts Bad taste as Powerhouse cookery book misses deadline Clair Weaver October 24, 2026 — 9:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Julie Gibbs was running Penguin’s lifestyle imprint Lantern, she declared cookbooks could take “anything from 18 months to four years” to complete. It was an estimate borne of experience: the cookbook guru had published big culinary names including Kylie Kwong, Matt Moran, Maggie Beer and Stephanie Alexander. “It is important to choose ideas with staying power,” she said. Today her comments, from an interview with digital publication The Design Files in 2013, have come back to bite her. Former cookbook publisher Julie Gibbs, who has been working on the Australian Culinary Archive for seven years. juliegibbs.com For the past seven years, Gibbs has been working on the Australian Culinary Archive: a $1.5 million dollar project supported by taxpayer funding that was supposed to culminate in a “landmark” book to coincide with the Powerhouse Parramatta’s much-anticipated opening on November 7. But the Herald can reveal there is no sign of the book, which has been in the works for four of those years. “The Powerhouse looks forward to launching the publication in 2027,” a spokesperson said.



Yet last year, the museum still hoped to meet the publication deadline. “To coincide with the launch of Powerhouse Parramatta, Powerhouse Publishing will release a landmark publication – The Australian Culinary Archive (working title),” it said in a description of the role of archive advisor published in March last year, which was awarded to Gibbs. In two separate roles published in October last year, the Powerhouse sought an editorial advisor and editorial support and proofreading services for “a 1000-page publication that documents the Australian Culinary Archive”. The project was described as “nearing completion”. (Left to right) Julie Gibbs, Kate Gibbs (food author and granddaughter of Margaret Fulton), Guy Grossi, Lisa Havilah, Neil Perry, Louise Keats, Suzanne Gibbs, Peter Gilmore and Kylie Kwong gathered to mark the launch of the Australian Culinary Archive in 2020. Louie Douvis According to the Powerhouse’s website, France-based Australian food writer Libby Travers has been collaborating with Gibbs on the book “over the past few years”. Travers wrote on her personal blog about a 2024 research trip to the elBulli museum in Spain.



“I was there to look at the ways in which culinary history and culture can be recorded and represented – a research trip for the book I am writing with the erudite and exceptional Julie Gibbs,” she wrote. “It is a book that will tell the story of the past 50 years of cooking in Australia via the Powerhouse Museum’s Culinary Archive.” A Powerhouse spokesperson confirmed Gibbs has been involved with developing the archive and book since 2019, while Travers was engaged to edit the book and then as editorial advisor but was not paid travel or research fees. “The archive has been under development for seven years ... at an average annual cost of $120k per year including acquisitions, fees, and domestic travel,” the spokesperson said. “A publication to present this archive is currently in development. This has been a four-year project. The total cost is about $165k per year including editorial, design, photography, typesetting, rights and clearances costs. The rights, clearances and permissions process has been complex as it relates to materials for items that are up to 50 years old and is ongoing.” These figures - totalling $840,000 for the archive and $660,000 for the book - do not include internal museum costs, such as staffing.



Related Article Exclusive

Arts Powerhouse slammed over Kylie Kwong’s new $440,000 ambassador role Questions over the book come amid heightened scrutiny on the museum over budget concerns. On October 13, the Herald revealed Kwong had been awarded a $440,000 contract to be a culinary ambassador for the Powerhouse a month after then CEO Lisa Havilah said her involvement was due to end. Kwong has previously had cookbooks published by Gibbs, who described the chef as “my bestie” on social media in 2014. The Herald does not suggest either of the women participated in wrongdoing. Havilah has stepped aside from her role pending “investigations into governance and procurement”, with NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin stepping in as acting CEO and NSW Treasury executive Cassandra Wilkinson parachuted in as chief operating officer. In 2020, it was estimated the archive would take “at least two years to collect” before items would be catalogued and digitised at the museum.



Whisk used by Damien Pignolet from the Australian Culinary Archive Powerhouse Designed to be “a living record of the people who have shaped Australia’s food culture”, it includes material from chefs, producers, vendors, writers, photographers, critics and diners. Objects collected include a whisk from Gibbs’ chef ex-husband Damian Pignolet, a label for chocolates sold by Sean Moran and a stool from Kwong’s restaurant Billy Kwong. Gibbs has had three contracts in her tenure at the Powerhouse. First she was head consultant for the archive, then an “artistic associate” as part of a controversial $2.6 million program that was terminated, and since last year archive advisor. Her current contract expires in July next year, with an option to extend it by another year. When she was awarded her first role, Gibbs told the Herald’s Good Food she felt “like the luckiest person in the world”, adding “I’m travelling all over Australia to interview incredibly influential people about the paths they’ve trodden and see what treasures are hiding in their storerooms and cupboards”. World.title: I try not to complain about crime in London – an ancestor of mine snatched and ran
World.content:
WorldEuropeLondon I try not to complain about crime in London – an ancestor of mine snatched and ran David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. London: The conditions look perfect when I walk up from the underground to search for London crime. The sun is out, and so are the crowds. The footpaths around the Bond Street tube station are jammed with shoppers heading to the big department stores nearby, while tourists linger at the souvenir stores. I can see why this neighbourhood is known for mobile phone theft. Some pedestrians are glancing at their screens as they walk, and some stop to take selfies along Oxford Street, holding their phones out near the kerb. That seems risky in a city with almost 200 cases of phone theft and robbery each day. Stan Blake, a former building worker who sells The Big Issue magazine along London’s Marylebone Lane, says he sees theft on most days. David Crowe But I’m searching for the scene of an older crime. I find it when I get to the corner of Oxford Street and Gee’s Court, a tiny passageway leading to a pedestrian mall. Here, two centuries ago, an ancestor of mine took up a common trade on these streets. He snatched and ran.



William Daley, 17, was a young Irish lad at work with an even younger accomplice. Together, they found a target on Oxford Street in the winter of 1818. England was at peace after defeating Napoleon, but London was ravaged by crushing poverty – and a small square of silk could be worth about two days’ wages. The target, George Reid, did not even notice the younger thief steal his handkerchief. But a worker nearby saw exactly what happened: the boy took the silk and passed it quickly to Daley, who slipped it into his hat and walked on in the hope of a swift getaway along Oxford Street. That walk turned into a run, however, when Reid called for help. “Stop, thief!” he yelled. A transcript from the trial of William Daley on theft charges at the Old Bailey in 1818, including the eyewitness accounts of the crime. He was sentenced to transportation to Australia for life. David Crowe Daley ran from Oxford Street towards Marylebone Lane, a curved street of stores and pubs. A policeman then made an arrest that changed history – at least in my family. “I heard the alarm, and saw the prisoner running up Marylebone Lane,” the constable told a court a few weeks later. “He was stopped, and the handkerchief fell out of his hat.” We know this because the Old Bailey, in a testament to British justice, kept the transcript from Daley’s appearance in court. The sentence for stealing a silk handkerchief with a value of seven shillings? “Transported for life.” Daley was on a ship to the colonies in July, and he arrived in Sydney on New Year’s Eve. He may not have felt like celebrating.



It seems like a story from Charles Dickens, although Oliver Twist did not appear until 20 years later. In that tale, the hero is found to be of high birth and inherits a fortune, but there was no secret family wealth for Daley. He was sent to work on the farms west of Sydney as a convict labourer before eventually gaining his ticket of leave. At least things did not end badly: he married, became a farmer and died at 70 near Windsor. Related Article Crime Is London finally winning its mobile phone theft war? I think about that life-changing punishment as I walk down Marylebone Lane. Some of the shop workers around here tell me they rarely see a thief being caught. One of the bar staff at the Spread Eagle, a nearby pub, says she sees a phone being stolen on most nights when she finishes her shift. A thief will speed past on an electric scooter or bike, snatch a phone and race away. The Metropolitan Police release videos showing brazen thefts in busy areas like Oxford Street, but they say they are cracking down. “Phone theft and robbery fell from 81,439 offences in 2024 to 71,867 in 2025,” they say. It looks like falling again this year, judging by the tally to August. This seems to add to the progress we reported last year. In one celebrated case, the victim of a phone theft helped guide police to a warehouse at Heathrow Airport using a “find my phone” feature. Remarkably, the phone was left on, and the location signal was still working, so police were able to arrest a gang responsible for shipping around 40,000 phones to China. The three men were sentenced last month to prison terms of up to nine years.



While the official numbers say things are getting better, it is hard to be sure. So I talk to someone who sees a lot of what happens on these streets. Stan Blake, 61, has been selling The Big Issue near Marylebone Lane for about three years. Raised in Wales, he was a builder but lost his job and now relies on magazine sales for his living. Related Article Opinion

Charity I was too busy for the charity vendor. But he said something that stopped me in my tracks Stephen Brook Special correspondent, The Age Just last week, he saw two police cars chasing a man on a scooter who had allegedly just stolen five phones. A few years ago, he watched in disbelief as a thief snatched the phone of a woman trying to pay for The Big Issue using Blake’s mobile payment device. He lent her his phone so she could call for help. Has he ever seen anyone chase a thief and recover a phone? “No, they’ve always got away,” he says. This is a key reason why mobile phone theft is such a talking point in London: many people are worried authorities are not bringing people to justice; that there is a breakdown in law and order. In a sense, the silk handkerchief was the mobile phone of its day: a small and relatively common item of high value. The difference is that today’s bikes and scooters seem to guarantee a quick escape. And with so many tourists in this city, the thieves are never short of targets.



I cannot say I like it, but I try not to complain about crime in London. Where would I be without it? Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: In her new book, Pachinko author Min Jin Lee takes on the tyranny of ambition
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature In her new book, Pachinko author Min Jin Lee takes on the tyranny of ambition Declan Fry October 24, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Speaking from her home in Harlem, New York, Min Jin Lee asks if it’s a good time to call. It’s a perfect time. Commiserating about time differences, I recall visiting a (very cold) Harlem years ago, where I accidentally mistook someone’s wash detergent for communal use. Min’s voice picks up at this juicy gossip. She has no New Yorker-berating to share (the woman at the laundromat really chewed me out) but she admits – despite everyone telling her it has an “attitude” – feeling that Melbourne is nice. Author Min Jin Lee. Hae Ran of Channel Yes “I love Australia. People are so open. You can get into a fight with someone in a train here by looking at them wrong. Everyone told me Melbourne is like the New York of Australia because they’re very artistic and intellectual and cool. They meant cool as in avant-garde – but they also meant it as in, a little more chilly,” she says, laughing.“People aren’t triggered at a laundromat by using 10 cents worth of soap. Then again, I do sort of assume in life that everyone is cooler than me.” Her contentment with not being the coolest person in the room speaks to the generosity that drives her. In her 2007 debut, Free Food for Millionaires, and 2017’s bestselling Pachinko, the fortunes of people striving to change their lives in a tumultuous world are the focus. At the heart of her new novel, American Hagwon, are the Kohs, a well-off family brought down in the world after the Asian financial crisis. As they move from Seoul to Sydney and then California through the 1990s and the early years of this century, their relationships are subject to the tyranny of distance. Boarding schools offer the opportunity for a new life but also distance from the family home. White-collar workers are liable to suddenly wind up working in fast food joints. Wherever the Koh children live – studious Bo, athletic DH, artistically minded Mido – education is not just a matter of aspiration but a continual struggle of re-evaluation and self-reflection. The hagwon, a Korean cram school, becomes symbolic of the promise of another life. Australia, Lee says, offered a fascinating social experiment in which to set much of the novel – especially as an alternative to the more ruthless aspects of American society. Among her affections in this regard she counts HECS, TAFE (“genius” for offering vocational rights sans university – “I was so, so impressed”) and mandatory voting (“the sausage sizzle!”).



“There’s a reason why even the coolest person in Melbourne is probably warmer and more relaxed than a New Yorker – [in the US] you have to bankrupt yourself to get your cancer treated. If I give a speech about violence against Asian-Americans, or lobby for reproductive rights, which is under threat in America, I pay the price of that as a writer,” she says. “It’s really difficult to survive. In America, if your employer doesn’t give you the time to vote, you can’t vote. To me, it’s not a true democracy.” She’s not unaware of the White Australia policy or Indigenous dispossession, she says. But truths coexist. Animating Min’s writing is her tangible sense of compassion. You don’t know what people are going through, she says. Someone may look fine but have troubles that are not visible on the surface. “I want to persuade people to recognise the full humanity of people who have been very invisible. I also wanted to show the lie behind it. You can have this highly selective education and yet end up working as a fried fish cook. You get old. No one wants you. I’m talking about being made obsolete in the era of capitalism.” Lee bemoans the loss of play and of third spaces, of less rabidly competitive and structured lives. It is possible – indeed almost normal now – to walk through streets where people wander alone, haloed by phone light, returning to homes whose other occupants have long since retreated to their own isolation. The world is becoming automated and predetermined in a way where even the attempt to escape isolation – to ask for a human being at a shop, to seek almost any form of human contact, physical or otherwise – is treated as a perverse eccentricity rather than an essential element of life.



“People need to play. It’s really sad when I hear someone ask, ‘how did you get your job? What did you do?’ As if they could reverse engineer the process. I look at them and I kind of think, ‘it doesn’t really work that way’. People are fairly circuitous. And the people who are good at what they do are often more circuitous,” she says with a laugh. “I’ve seen so many people with selective education break down. They tend to be the most direct, process-wise. You think they’ll go far in life. And it just does not work out. ” I mention that a character like Mido – who has no intention of entering the theatre but finds, when she begins writing scenes in Sydney, that she is forced to think about everyone else in the scene and even the people offstage – connects to one of the book’s epigraphs: a 1963 James Baldwin lecture about how, as one is educated, one begins examining the society in which one lives. Min Jin Lee in New York last month. Getty Images for Spotify “Yes! Oh my gosh, that scene was such a hard one to write. My novels are Trojan horses. I really am trying so hard to say, ‘please look at this’. Please look at how we are destroying ourselves. It’s a radical gesture just to live the life you didn’t think you could live. We lose so much when we have cynical young people who have been heartbroken by what our generation has delivered to them. I really do think it’s possible to fix this. But it’s going to take us older people reaching out to them. We have to take care of children who are not our children.” The seduction of believing that education – a nice job, a certain decision – can protect or shelter you is precarious, Lee says. Especially in neoliberal environments where, in the absence of regulation, the conditions of life and existence itself “can become a kind of hell”.



“The only people I really saw survive the IMF crisis who didn’t have generational wealth – which destroyed so many paths – are those who would choose a different path.” Lee interviewed many people in writing the book, she says. She met people like John, the family patriarch, cornered by economic crises out of their control. Many of those who fell came from the middle class, people who had been taught to believe in the promises of the social compact. “Literature all the time is saying: look at the character. Look at the context. I want to know what people are doing when no one’s looking. And also look at the fact there are so many contradictions.” Related Article Review Need a new book? Our picks of the latest fiction and non-fiction books Yet research has limits, and the imagination has to go where research cannot. In size and scope, American Hagwon is comparable to the big, baggy monsters of 19th-century realism. Balzac’s Human Comedy. Zola. Like the celebrated novels of that era, it is also a story of class and upward mobility. Unlike them, though, it is written in a plainspoken style. Lee describes the precision of its sentences – what she calls “clean” writing – as acting in service to the delivery of the message. She looks to the nonfiction of Joan Didion and V.S. Naipaul, she says, to find ways of delivering the same immersive qualities of authors like Zola and Hardy without their grand, omniscient narrative style. “I want it to be so clean that there’s actually no room for misinterpretation. I’d like it if you don’t even think about me. To just be about the story.” Before she has to go, we talk about some of our shared loves. “I like dogs,” she says. “I like children. I think adults are kind of scary sometimes, but mostly they mean well. That’s the way I look at things.”



Truer words have never been spoken. American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee (4th Estate, $38) is available now. What else is happening in the book world? Homicide squad detectives have extradited a man from Poland and charged him with murder over the death of a man whose body was discovered inside a metal cabinet floating in a creek on the NSW Mid North Coast in 2023.

Two men have previously been sentenced over the death of Darcy Schafer-Turner, who was 22 when he disappeared following a drug-related dispute.

Homicide Squad detectives on Friday with the man extradited from Poland. He has been charged with murder. NSW Police

Zachary Richard Fraser was sentenced to 6½ years in prison in 2025 after pleading guilty to the manslaughter of Schafer-Turner, who was his close school friend, at a unit in Peakhurst.

The court heard Fraser taped his mouth shut while another man held Schafer-Turner in a chokehold. Schafer-Turner lost consciousness and suffocated.

World.title: Deadly shooting outside Paris a ‘terrorist attack’, say police
World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime Deadly shooting outside Paris a ‘terrorist attack’, say police David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 6:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: A gunman has killed one victim and wounded five others in an outer suburb of Paris known for its migrant communities, prompting public warnings of a terror attack in the wake of violent protests. Police arrested the alleged killer after a frenzy of drive-by shootings that left one 12-year-old girl fighting for her life. Forensic investigators search for evidence after a shooting in Trappes, outside Paris. AP French President Emmanuel Macron described the shootings as a “racist terrorist attack” in the areas of Trappes and Yvelines, south-west of the Paris city centre, and warned of the pressure on the nation from weeks of unrest. Police said they were treating the attack as terrorism and were aware of reports that the killer had set traps in his home to kill visitors that he expected to investigate him after the shootings. Police also detained one of his family members.



The shootings on Friday (French time) came on the eve of another series of protests and rallies due to be held on Saturday in Paris and other cities over the cost of living and school funding. Worried about another outbreak of violence and looting, the French government has mobilised 70,000 police to guard against rioting, while authorities in Lyon and Marseilles have banned the marches. French President Emmanuel Macron meets community members at the town hall in Trappes after the shooting. Reuters Authorities did not draw a direct link between the riots and the shootings, but the attack in the Paris suburbs came after a week of debate about whether migrants were among the looters who smashed stores last weekend. Macron spoke of a “turning point in our republic and our nation” as a result of the terror attack.



Mayor Nicolas Dainville, whose local government of La Verriere includes Yvelines, said the attack was another sign of the pressure on French unity after the protests. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated “A racist motive seems clear, given that here in La Verriere three individuals of African descent were targeted,” he told Franceinfo. “This points to a very serious situation in France, a country that is fractured and divided. “The atmosphere we are currently living in – in which the mayors, in their own modest way, are trying to address – is truly critical.”



National police union spokesman Rudy Manna told Franceinfo the gunman fired multiple times at people walking on the street who had done nothing to provoke him. Manna said the evidence suggested the gunman also intended to kill a police officer. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned on Friday about the risk of further violence in protests on Saturday, accusing ultra-left groups of encouraging violence and looting. More than 3000 stores were damaged or looted last weekend after protests turned violent across the country. Police arrested 2700 people, about 70 per cent of them adults.



Related Article Analysis

Paris protests The violence of the streets of Paris looked like rage. It revealed a society that will take years to heal “We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence,” Nunez told reporters on Friday after meetings with Macron and other government leaders. Nunez said authorities had identified online calls from hard-left groups that encouraged activists to target public buildings. “We are not ​talking about a nice, friendly demonstration,” he said. “We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and ⁠we will let absolutely nothing pass.”



Police have authorised ​a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday but have insisted it take place away from the Place de la Republique, an area that was a focal point of the riots last weekend and has been under curfew since then. Authorities rejected requests for rallies in Paris by the main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018. Many French cities beyond Paris have also banned protests, including France’s second- and third-largest cities, Marseille and Lyon. Nunez ‌said 10,000 more ⁠police would be on the streets than a week ago. With Reuters

World.title: Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk
World.content:
Perspective PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk Matt Dennien October 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Approaching the halfway milestone of Queensland’s four-year electoral cycle, Premier David Crisafulli has spent the past week doing plenty of talking – in speech after set-piece speech. He has spent it talking about what his government has done, and what it’s yet to do. The latter involves fixing the more nebulous “crises” he rode to power vowing to address. “The big four issues that I spoke about before the election remain the big four issues and the big four challenges,” Crisafulli said at his 2026 CEDA State of the State address on Monday. Over a week of speeches, Premier David Crisafulli stayed resolutely on message. AAPIMAGE “And on all of them [health, housing, crime and cost of living], we are making progress after a long period of time where the numbers went in the wrong direction.”



While Crisafulli can cite numbers heading in a better direction – and did, across several other major speeches this week, including to the property and local government sectors – more than anyone else, he should know the limits of relying on statistics. During a Queensland Media Club appearance on Wednesday billed as featuring a “significant policy announcement” in the law and order space, no such thing came, beyond confirmation the parliament will pass a government bill next week. Nor was there anything new in any other area. ‘I want to talk today about what I call a trio of opportunities: fuel, critical minerals, and data centres. All three have challenges. All three have opportunities.’ Crisafulli in his Monday State of the State speech This is the bind in which the government now finds itself: a list of concrete election platform items already all-but ticked off, leaving them either pushing ahead with new policy efforts in areas plaguing governments across the country and globe, or hoping its “let us cook” line finds sympathy. s are still running for the work of the “new Queensland government”, but frustrations over this positioning are beginning to emerge – particularly on crime, where the LNP set the terms of the debate while in opposition, yet admits that public dissatisfaction remains, two years on.





Crisafulli and his strategists seem to believe these glimpses beyond the pre-election picture they painted are too minor to spook a wider population wary of action that’s too swift or extreme. The Labor opposition, led for now by Steven Miles, seems stuck on a small-target strategy, hoping that something – or an accumulation of things – will suddenly become too much for people to bear. The resignation from cabinet of Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm may be the first bit of bark taken from Crisafulli that Labor would view as a win. While Crisafulli’s LNP remain the clear favourites in this masthead’s regular Resolve Political Monitor, that polling also shows the broader mood has soured across a year that has thrown no shortage of extra problems at households and governments.



After significant improvement following the 2024 vote, the outlook for the next year or so among those surveyed for both their personal lives, and the state more broadly, has since returned to pre-election levels. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership Almost more people think things will get worse in their lives than not change, and both cohorts are double the size of those who think it will get better. Compared to before the election, their view of the state’s future is now more pessimistic. The tectonic plates long holding the two-party system in place appear their shakiest since Queensland saw Pauline Hanson’s best yet showing in an Australian parliament three decades ago. So two years could be a long time – for all involved. How do you act, or give the appearance of acting, on fundamental social and economic problems in a way that makes people feel things have changed for the better, when you are also cautious of moving too fast or too far, let alone actually change things for the long-term good?



The Crisafulli government may have a swathe of state and national elections across the country to learn from before it has to face voters for the first time from office, but a bet on people’s willingness to wait to feel change while being told it is happening is no longer such a sure thing. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
